Explication: The two powers surrounding the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century. Byzantium (Eastern Roman Empire) and the Sassanids (Zoroastrian Persian Empire) were exhausting themselves in an endless war, clearing the way for Arab conquests.
Community of Muslim believers, transcending tribal boundaries. All Muslims form a single body regardless of their origin.
Arabic term literally meaning "effort". Refers to the inner effort for self-improvement and the armed defense of the community.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Definitive break between the Roman Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church, over papal authority and the Filioque question. This schism made relations between Byzantium and Rome complex at the time when Alexios I was requesting military aid.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Byzantine Emperor who sent an embassy to Pope Urban II to request mercenaries against the Seljuk Turks. His modest request unintentionally triggered the massive mobilization of the first crusade.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Total remission of the punishments due to sins, granted by the Pope. Urban II promised one to all crusade participants - a powerful driver for mobilization in a deeply religious society.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Nomadic people from Central Asia who swept into Europe around 370, pushing the Goths and other Germanic peoples to cross Roman borders to flee. Their leader Attila would ravage Europe in the 450s.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Treaty by which Rome authorized a Barbarian people to settle on its territory in exchange for military service. The Visigoths obtained a foedus in 382, but Rome did not respect it, which explains Alaric's revolt.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Terme: The division of the Empire in 395
Explication: Upon the death of Theodosius I, the Empire was shared between his two sons: Honorius in the West (capital Ravenna) and Arcadius in the East (Constantinople). This permanent division weakened the response to invasions.

Politics entity born from The Coronation of Charlemagne (800), claiming to embody the continuity of the Roman Empire in the West under Christian authority. It lasted until 1806 and structured the Germanic space for a thousand years.

Carolingian "envoys of the master": royal inspectors sent in pairs (one bishop, one layman) to control local administration and render justice in the name of the emperor. Key instrument of Carolingian government over an immense territory.

English scholar brought in by Charlemagne to lead the Palatine School in Aachen. He oversaw the reform of writing and education, training a generation of literate administrators who maintained the empire.

Medieval organization based on personal ties: the suzerain grants land (fief) in exchange for military service and loyalty. The Magna Carta (1215) was extracted within this contractual framework: the barons reminded the king of his obligations.
Major Event where John Lackland lost his possessions to Philip II Augustus, provoking the fiscal crisis at the origin of the Magna Carta (1215).

Legal principle protecting against arbitrary arrests: any person arrested must be presented to a judge. Direct heritage of clause 39 of the Magna Carta (1215), it has become a pillar of Anglo-Saxon law.

Medieval medical belief that diseases were caused by impure vapors emanating from stagnant waters and corpses. It explains the total helplessness of medicine against the Plague - one could not treat what one did not understand.

Genoa and Venice, whose commercial ships linked the Black Sea to Europe, were the vectors of the epidemic. Genoese ships introduced the plague to Sicily in 1347, spreading the bacteria through their Mediterranean trade networks.

Accused of poisoning wells, tens of thousands of Jews were massacred in Germany and France during the Plague. Pope Clement VI defended them but was little heard in devastated cities looking for scapegoats.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: Agreement by which Charles VI of France disinherits his son, the Dauphin Charles, in favor of the King of England Henry V, creating a Franco-English dynastic union.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: Ceremony by which the King of France was anointed with holy oil, conferring upon him a quasi-sacred character. Only a king crowned in Reims was fully legitimate in the eyes of the Church and the people - hence the urgency for Joan to lead Charles VII there.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: French faction allied with the English, led by the Duke of Burgundy (Philip the Good in 1429). Their alliance with England was broken by the Treaty of Arras in 1435.

Terme: The sack of Constantinople by the 4th Crusade (1204)
Explication: The crusaders, diverted by Venice, looted Christian Constantinople for three days in 1204. This trauma permanently weakened Byzantium and explains Byzantine mistrust of the West during the siege of 1453.

Terme: The Greek diaspora and the Renaissance
Explication: Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople brought their manuscripts to Italy, contributing decisively to the Renaissance. The fall of Byzantium paradoxically accelerated the intellectual revival of the West.

Constantinople had preserved and transmitted Roman law, Greek philosophy, and Christian theology for a thousand years. Its fall put an end to this living continuity between Antiquity and the modern world.

Aztec myth: the universe has already been created and destroyed four times. The current fifth sun is only kept alive through human sacrifices. This cosmology made sacrifices cosmically necessary - without them, the sun would stop.

"Floating gardens" created in Lake Texcoco: artificial islands of mud and vegetation allowing for highly productive agriculture. Tenochtitlán was surrounded by a network of canals and cultivated lands that fed 200,000 inhabitants.

Aztec capital founded in 1325 on an islet in Lake Texcoco, where Mexico City is located today. It was one of the largest cities in the world in 1519, with a sophisticated network of aqueducts and canals.
The triumph of the capture of Granada released resources and created a momentum of national ambition that explains Isabella of Castile's support for Columbus.
Florentine navigator who understood that the discovered lands were an unknown continent. The continent was named in his honor in 1507.
Agreement arbitrated by the Pope dividing the world into two spheres of influence between Spain (west) and Portugal (east).

Terme: The Ancien Régime and the three estates
Explication: French society divided into three estates: Clergy (1st), Nobility (2nd), and Third Estate (97% of the population, 3rd). At the Estates General, each estate had only one vote out of three, despite the overwhelming demographic representativeness of the Third Estate.

Royal order of imprisonment without trial or explanation, signed by the king. The Bastille symbolized this royal arbitrariness, even though in July 1789 it contained only 7 prisoners - its value was purely symbolic.

An autonomous military unit of 15,000 to 30,000 men including all arms, capable of fighting alone for several days. This organizational innovation allowed for the speed of maneuver that was Napoleon's strength.
Nelson's decisive naval victory over the Franco-Spanish fleet, the same week as Ulm. It put an end to the plans to invade England and explains why Napoleon could never defeat British maritime power.
Napoleonic economic politics (1806) forbidding all European trade with England, to ruin it economically. Its imperfect application forced Napoleon to invade the Iberian Peninsula and then Russia.

Meeting of European powers to rebuild the post-Napoleonic order. It redrew the map of Europe, restored monarchies, and created the "European Concert" which maintained a relative peace for almost a century.
Pact signed in 1815 between Russia, Austria, and Prussia to defend monarchical principles against revolutionary ideas. It was the instrument for suppressing liberal uprisings of the 1820s-1830s.

Nicknamed "the bravest of the brave," he led the French cavalry at Waterloo. His disastrous charge against the British squares, launched too early without artillery support, was one of the fatal tactical mistakes of the day.

Conflict triggered by Napoleon III, ending with the crushing defeat at Sedan and the capture of the Emperor. The humiliating capitulation and the siege of Paris created the breeding ground for the Commune.

Head of the provisional government in Versailles who ordered the crushing of the Commune during the "Bloody Week" (May 21-28, 1871). A former journalist and historian, he was the first president of the Third Republic.

Organization founded in London in 1864, bringing together trade unions and workers' parties from several countries. Although the Commune was not its direct work, Marx celebrated it as the first experience of workers' power.

A Jewish officer, Alfred Dreyfus, was wrongly convicted of espionage by an anti-Semitic general staff. The affair tore France apart between Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards, revealing deep tensions within French society.

Meeting of European powers to settle the partition of Africa without war among themselves. In a few decades, Europe colonized 90% of the African continent, drawing arbitrary borders that still cause conflicts today.
Philosophy according to which science will solve all human problems. The dominant doctrine of the Belle Époque, it explains the optimism of this period and its brutal shattering by the war of 1914.
Franco-British offensive launched on July 1, 1916, to relieve Verdun. It caused 60,000 British casualties on the first day alone — the deadliest day in British military history.

Since 1914, the Western Front had stabilized into a network of trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland. This positional warfare explains why battles like Verdun were fought over a few square kilometers for months.

Terme: The heavy artillery of the Great War
Explication: Artillery accounted for 60-70% of First World War casualties. Technical progress since 1870 had made offensive weapons far more powerful than defenses, creating the trench impasse.

A Siberian healer monk who gained the influence of Tsarina Alexandra by relieving the hemophilic crises of Tsarevich Alexei. His alleged political interference and scandalous image deeply discredited the imperial court.

An ideology combining Marx's economic theories (class struggle, exploitation of the proletariat) and Lenin's tactical innovations (disciplined avant-garde party, organized revolution). This was the ideology of the Bolsheviks who took power in October 1917.

A council of workers' and soldiers' delegates, elected in factories and barracks. In 1917, it effectively controlled the streets and the army, creating an unstable "double power" in the face of the legal provisional government.

A monetary system where currencies were convertible into gold at a fixed rate, limiting the ability of states to create money. It mechanically spread the American crisis to the entire World: when the United States reduced their money supply, all countries linked to gold suffered.

A set of American programs combining economic stimulus (large-scale public works), financial reform (FDIC, SEC), and social protection. It did not end the crisis but created the foundations of the American Providence State.

The practice of borrowing from one's bank to buy shares, betting on their rise. Very widespread in the 1920s, it amplified the bubble and, during the crash, forced millions of Americans to sell urgently to repay their loans.

The invasion of the USSR by Germany: 3 million soldiers on a 3,000 km front - the largest military operation in history. The failure to take Moscow in 1941 forced Hitler to refocus his effort towards the south and Caucasian oil in 1942.

Commander of the surrounded German 6th Army. Hitler made him Field Marshal on January 30, 1943, to encourage him to die rather than surrender. Paulus capitulated the following day, becoming the first German Field Marshal to be captured alive.

Soviet counter-offensive (November 19, 1942) that encircled the 300,000 soldiers of the 6th Army in a giant pincer movement. Planned by Zhukov and Vasilevsky, it transformed the fierce defense of Stalingrad into a decisive strategic victory.

A reaction in which the nucleus of a heavy atom (uranium 235, plutonium 239) splits, releasing colossal energy and new neutrons that trigger a chain reaction. This is the principle of the atomic bomb.

Stalin declared war on Japan exactly on the day of the Nagasaki bomb, invading Manchuria. Some historians believe that this Soviet threat was as decisive as the bombs in the Japanese decision to surrender.

A syndrome caused by exposure to radiation: nausea, hair loss, internal hemorrhaging, immune failure. Tens of thousands of survivors died in the following weeks from this disease, which was then unknown to doctors.

National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909 to defend civil rights through legal means. Rosa Parks was an active member and had undergone civil disobedience training long before her famous gesture.

Set of state laws establishing racial segregation in the American South after 1877. Their name comes from a stereotypical minstrel show Figure. They organized total separation in schools, transportation, hospitals and all public spaces.

US Supreme Court ruling declaring segregation in public schools unconstitutional. This decision gave legal momentum to the Civil Rights Movement and explains why Montgomery was then also challenged in the courts.

Nuclear doctrine stating that neither the United States nor the USSR could survive a nuclear war. This logic of balanced terror deterred everyone from attacking and structures the entire dynamic of the Cuban crisis.

Failed invasion attempt of Cuba by Cuban exiles trained by the CIA. The humiliating failure weakened Kennedy, encouraged Khrushchev to take risks and strengthened Castro, creating the conditions for the 1962 crisis.

American nuclear missiles installed in Turkey in 1961, within reach of the USSR. The final secret agreement included their discreet withdrawal - a concession that Kennedy kept secret for decades so as not to appear to be yielding to Soviet blackmail.

Unlike the protectorates (Morocco, Tunisia), Algeria had been three French departments since 1848. Any independence therefore legally amounted to an amputation of national territory - hence the intensity of the politics conflict in the metropole.

Coup d'état attempt by four generals opposed to independence. De Gaulle crushed it in four days thanks to a radio speech. It was followed by the creation of the OAS, a pro-French Algeria terrorist organization.

Nickname for settlers of European origin living in Algeria. Nearly a million of them had to leave the country in 1962 under traumatic conditions, abandoning their homes under the threat 'the suitcase or the coffin'.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: Strategy of weak forces against a technically superior army: avoid pitched battles, harass the enemy, use the terrain and popular support, exhaust the opponent over the long term. The Viet-Minh excelled at it throughout the Indochina War.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: Accords ending the Indochina War: Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel. Reunification elections scheduled for 1956 were never held, sowing the seeds of the American war that was to follow.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: General-in-chief of the Viet-Minh, former self-taught history teacher in strategy. His genius was to have dozens of heavy cannons transported by hand and bicycle up the hills overlooking Dien Bien Phu - a logistical feat considered impossible.

Terme: The Young Turks (Committee of Union and Progress)
Explication: Turkish nationalist Movement that overthrew Sultan Abdul Hamid II in 1908. The Enver-Talaat-Cemal triumvirate, extremist nationalists, organized the genocide in the context of the war, in a project for an "ethnically pure Turkey".

First wave of Armenian massacres under Sultan Abdul Hamid II, causing between 100,000 and 300,000 deaths. This unsanctioned precedent showed future Ottoman authorities that such crimes could go unpunished.

The term "genocide" was coined by legal scholar Raphael Lemkin in 1944 specifically with Armenians in mind. The UN Convention (1948) defines it as the intent to destroy "in whole or in part" a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Meeting between Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin laying the foundations of the post-war world order: division of Europe into zones of influence, conditions for Soviet entry against Japan, structure of the UN to be created.

Terme: Veto power in the Security Council
Explication: Each of the 5 permanent members can block any Council resolution with a single "no" vote. This mechanism paralyzed the Council during the Cold War and continues with Russia and China on many contemporary crises.

The UN's judicial organ based in The Hague, which settles disputes between States. Unlike the ICC (which judges individuals), it judges States. Its decisions are binding but it has no enforcement mechanism.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Explication: After three wars in 70 years, France and Germany had made their rivalry the main driver of European conflicts. The ECSC and then the Élysée Treaty (1963) sealed a friendship that became the engine of all European integration.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Explication: Founding treaty of the European Union creating European citizenship, launching the single currency process (the euro in 2002), establishing a common foreign policy and strict economic convergence criteria.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Terme: The four freedoms of the single market
Explication: Free movement of goods, people, services, and capital - foundations of the common market of the Treaty of Rome. They represent the deepest economic integration ever achieved between sovereign States.
Peace agreement between the Hutu government and the RPF (Rwandan Patriotic Front). Hutu extremists, refusing any power-sharing, organized the genocide to prevent it from being implemented.

The UN Mission commanded by the Canadian general Roméo Dallaire had 2,500 soldiers on site. Dallaire warned the UN as early as January 1994 of an impending genocide, but was forbidden to act. Its inaction is today considered a historical failure.

Terme: Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines (RTLM)
Explication: Hutu extremist radio station that, during the genocide, broadcast live lists of people to be killed and called for the extermination of Tutsis, described as "cockroaches." It constituted a major tool for coordinating the massacres.

Nom du cours: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
Explication: Gorbachev's reforms starting from 1986: glasnost (transparency) allowed criticism of the Soviet regime, perestroika (restructuring) attempted to reform the economy. They unintentionally destabilized the entire Soviet bloc.

Nom du cours: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
Explication: Liberal reform of communism in Czechoslovakia, crushed by the invasion of Soviet tanks. Gorbachev's decision not to repeat this intervention in 1989 was therefore historically revolutionary.

Nom du cours: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
Explication: General Secretary of the GDR since 1971, he had declared that the Wall would last "another 50 or 100 years." Replaced on October 18, 1989, just before the fall of the Wall, he died in exile in Chile in 1994.

Line of fortifications built by France in the 1930s along the Franco-German border. The Blitzkrieg bypassed it through the Belgian Ardennes, supposed to be impassable for tanks - making the Maginot Line totally useless.

General von Manstein's plan: concentrate armored units in the Ardennes to break through the center and reach the English Channel, encircling the Franco-British armies engaged in Belgium. Bold and risky, this plan was a total success.

Maritime evacuation of 338,000 Franco-British soldiers surrounded at Dunkirk by an improvised flotilla of military and civilian vessels. This "miracle" allowed Great Britain to continue the war, but left France without an army.

Truman's speech (March 1947) asserting that the United States would support any people resisting "subjugation by outside pressures." It marked the official beginning of the Cold War and the politics of containment of communism.

International communist organization created by Stalin in response to the Marshall Plan, to coordinate European communist parties. It forced Czechoslovakia and Poland, which had accepted Marshall aid, to refuse it.

"Economic miracle" of West Germany: between 1950 and 1960, its GDP tripled, moving from an economy in ruins to the leading European economic power. Partly funded by the Marshall Plan and favored by the 1948 monetary reform.

American foreign politics theory according to which if one country became communist, its neighbors would fall one after another. It justified the commitment in Vietnam to "stop communist progression in Southeast Asia."

Simultaneous attack by the Viet Cong on more than 100 American cities during the Vietnamese New Year. Militarily a failure for Hanoi, it destroyed the credibility of the Johnson administration in the United States.

Nationalist and communist leader, founder of the Viet-Minh (1941), first president of North Vietnam. His popular legitimacy as a liberator against the Japanese then the French gave him a politics advantage that the United States could never match.

Legal category invented at Nuremberg to designate the persecution and extermination of civilians. Unlike war crimes, they apply even in times of peace and have no statute of limitations. Nuremberg distinguished them for the first time.

Principle established at Nuremberg: individuals can be judged for international crimes even if they were acting on behalf of a State. "Obeying orders" is not an admissible defense - a founding principle of international criminal law.

Heir to the Nuremberg Principles, created in 2002 by the Rome Statute to judge genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. 124 countries have ratified it, but not the United States, Russia or China.

Joint Roosevelt-Churchill declaration affirming the right of peoples to self-determination. Used by independence movements as an argument against their colonizers, it created an ideological contradiction that empires could not resolve.

First meeting of independent Asian and African countries (29 nations), affirming the principles of non-alignment and anti-colonialism. It marked the birth of the "Third World" as an international politics force.
Term describing the forms of economic and politics domination exercised by former colonial powers over their formally independent ex-colonies, via multinationals, debt, and military bases.

"Homelands" to which Black people were assigned according to their ethnic group under apartheid. These non-viable territories represented 13% of South African territory for 80% of the population - a total geographical segregation.
Police opened fire on a peaceful demonstration against pass laws, killing 69 people. The global shock led to the banning of the ANC and pushed Mandela to create the armed wing of the resistance.

Instituted after 1994, it allowed perpetrators of apartheid crimes to obtain amnesty in exchange for a full public confession. Presided over by Desmond Tutu, it chose national reconciliation rather than trials.

Program of forced collectivization launched by Mao which caused the greatest famine in human history: between 15 and 55 million deaths. Its failure explains Mao's political sidelining and his need to regain control via the Cultural Revolution.

Revolutionary youth mobilized by Mao to attack the "four olds". They humiliated millions of teachers, doctors, intellectuals, and Party cadres during public sessions of criticism and forced self-confession.
Twice purged during the Cultural Revolution, he became the de facto leader of China after Mao's death (1976) and the father of economic reforms. His pragmatism transformed China into a global power.

Nom du cours: The Holocaust: mechanisms of a genocide
Explication: A meeting of 15 high-ranking Nazi officials where the "Final Solution" was planned and coordinated: the systematic extermination of Europe's Jews through death camps. It showed that the genocide was a bureaucratically organized state decision.

Nom du cours: The Holocaust: mechanisms of a genocide
Explication: SS mobile extermination units that followed the army during the invasion of the USSR. They shot approximately 1.5 million Soviet Jews. The Babi Yar massacre (33,771 deaths in two days) is the most famous example.

Nom du cours: The Holocaust: mechanisms of a genocide
Explication: A philosophical concept developed during the Eichmann trial: the worst crimes can be committed by ordinary, bureaucratic individuals who "do their job" without reflecting on the moral consequences of their actions.
The United States armed the Afghan mujahideen to fight the Soviets. These Islamist networks, particularly Bin Laden's, trained and financed during the Cold War, subsequently became Al-Qaeda.

A terrorist organization founded by Osama bin Laden in 1988 to fight the Soviets in Afghanistan. Its vision: a global war against the West and the corrupt Arab regimes supported by it. September 11 was its largest operation.

American invasion based on false information about weapons of mass destruction. It destabilized the Middle East, dismantled Iraqi state structures, and created the vacuum in which the Islamic State (ISIS) emerged.

Athenian statesman elected archon in 594 BC to resolve a social crisis. He canceled debts, abolished debt slavery, and reorganized the city by wealth rather than birth - the first step toward democracy.

Athenian reformer (508-507 BC) considered the true founder of democracy. He reorganized the city into 10 mixed geographical tribes, breaking traditional family solidarities in favor of political citizenship.
Athenian procedure by which citizens could vote to exile for 10 years a man deemed dangerous to democracy. Names were written on pottery shards (ostrakon). Its objective was preventive, not punitive.

Lincoln's decree freeing slaves in the Confederate States. It transformed the war into a moral crusade against slavery, prevented Great Britain from recognizing the Confederacy, and opened the army to Black soldiers.

Terme: States' rights vs. the federal government
Explication: Fundamental tension in American politics: Southern states claimed their right to decide for themselves on slavery against federal authority. This question structured the U.S. Constitution and continues to define American political debate.

Post-war period where the Southern states were placed under federal military control and the civil rights of former slaves were established. Its abandonment in 1877 led to the Jim Crow laws which lasted until the 1960s.

Phenomenon by which small molecules in the atmosphere scatter short wavelengths (blue, violet) much more than long ones (red). Described by Lord Rayleigh in 1871, it also explains why sunsets are red and orange.
White sunlight is composed of all the colors of the rainbow (from 380 nm for violet to 700 nm for red). Each color corresponds to a different wavelength that interacts differently with matter.

Sleep phase characterized by rapid eye movements, muscle paralysis, and intense brain activity close to wakefulness. This is the phase where the majority of dreams occur and where memory consolidation is most active.

For Freud (The Interpretation of Dreams, 1900), dreams express repressed desires in symbolic form. This theory is now widely criticized by neurosciences, which instead attribute them a role in memory and emotional consolidation.

Weak forces of attraction between water molecules, due to the polarity of the H₂O molecule. They establish themselves in an orderly fashion in ice, creating an airy crystalline structure — more voluminous than liquid water, and therefore less dense.

Contrary to almost all substances, water is denser at 4°C than at 0°C. When cooling from 4°C to 0°C, it expands. This anomaly is essential to aquatic life: ice floats and insulates the liquid water beneath it.

Terme: The hydrological cycle and salt accumulation
Explication: Water evaporates from the oceans, leaving salts behind. It falls back as rain, dissolves minerals from rocks, and transports them back to the oceans via rivers. This accumulation process has been ongoing for 4 billion years.

Global system of deep ocean currents driven by differences in temperature and salinity. Dense salinity causes cold water to sink, creating a "conveyor belt" that transports heat around the globe and regulates the climate.

Earth's axis tilted at 23.5° relative to its orbital plane - and not the distance to the Sun - causes the seasons. The same tilt always points toward the North Star, creating alternatively solstices and equinoxes.

Orbital points closest (perihelion, in January) and farthest (aphelion, in July) from the Sun. The difference in distance is 5%, too small to explain the seasons. Paradoxically, the northern winter coincides with the perihelion.

The cross-sectional shape of the wing, with a curved upper surface and a flatter lower surface. This asymmetry forces the air to move faster above than below, creating a pressure difference that generates lift.

In a fluid in movement, where the speed increases, the pressure decreases. The air moving faster on the upper surface of the wing exerts less pressure than on the lower surface, creating an upward "suction" that lifts the plane.
Most serious current Theory: yawning cools the brain by inhaling fresh air and stretching cranial vessels. This would explain why we yawn more when the ambient temperature is high.

Contagious yawning is linked to mirror neurons and contagiousness that mimic observed behaviors. Humans are more sensitive to the yawns of people they know, and autistic children are less sensitive to them - evidence of a link with empathy.

A sea-horse-shaped brain structure in the temporal lobe, essential for the formation of new conscious memories. Its surgical removal (case H.M.) results in a total inability to form new memories, without erasing old ones.

Cognitive system that temporarily maintains a small amount of information (7±2 items) available for current processing. Managed by the Prefrontal cortex, it is limited in capacity and duration (a few seconds without repetition).

Branch of the autonomic nervous system that prepares the body for action ("fight or flight"). Faced with a threat, it triggers adrenaline, accelerates the heart, dilates the pupils, and contracts the arrector pili muscles - the chills of fear.

A molecule with one hydrophilic end (water-loving) and one hydrophobic end (fat-loving). This dual nature allows it to insert itself into the lipid membranes of viruses and physically disintegrate them.

Certain viruses (coronavirus, influenza, HIV) are surrounded by a fatty membrane. This is their weak point: soap dissolves it, destroying the virus. Non-enveloped viruses (norovirus, poliovirus) are more resistant to soap.

Terme: Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain
Explication: Oxford researchers who purified penicillin starting in 1939 and tested it on humans in 1941. Without their work, Fleming's discovery would have remained a laboratory curiosity. They shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming.

An evolutionary phenomenon by which bacteria develop mechanisms to resist antibiotics. Predicted by Fleming as early as 1945, it now kills 1.27 million people per year - one of the main health threats of the 21st century.

Nom du cours: The discovery of electricity and its applications
Explication: Self-taught British physicist who discovered electromagnetic induction (1831): a varying magnetic field generates an electric current. This principle is the basis of all modern electric generators and transformers.

Nom du cours: The discovery of electricity and its applications
Terme: The War of Currents (Edison vs. Tesla)
Explication: Edison championed direct current (DC), Tesla and Westinghouse alternating current (AC). AC won because it can be transported over long distances. Edison organized public electrocutions of animals to demonstrate the "danger" of AC.

Röntgen and his first users were unaware of the dangers of X-rays. Doctors developed cancers after years of exposure. Marie Curie herself died of aplastic anemia caused by her years of contact with radioactive materials.

Terme: The "Little Curies" during World War I
Explication: Marie Curie equipped 20 mobile radiography trucks that traveled the French front, saving countless lives by making it possible to locate bullets without exploratory surgery. These vehicles were nicknamed "little Curies".

Nom du cours: The discovery of the microwave (by accident)
Explication: A self-taught engineer at Raytheon, orphaned at 18 months, with no degree. His curiosity led him to test magnetrons on food after feeling his chocolate bar melt. He filed several hundred patents during his career.

Astronomer (1571-1630) who empirically established the three laws of planetary Movement: elliptical orbits, equal areas, Period Square proportional to the semi-major axis. Newton built his Law of gravitation by providing the unifying theoretical explanation.

General Relativity (1915) surpassed Newton: gravity is not a force but a curvature of space-time caused by mass. It predicts phenomena that Newton could not explain: the precession of Mercury, the deflection of light, gravitational waves.
French physicist who discovered radioactivity in 1896 almost by accident: uranium salts had fogged a photographic plate through black paper. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize with the Curies.

Spontaneous phenomenon by which an unstable atomic nucleus transforms by emitting particles (alpha, beta) or radiation (gamma). Marie Curie understood that radioactivity was a property of the atom itself, not a chemical reaction.

A set of rules defining how data is broken down into packets, addressed, transmitted, and reassembled. Invented by Cerf and Kahn (1974), it is the "universal language" that allows heterogeneous networks to communicate with each other.

The first Soviet artificial satellite, its launch created a shockwave in the United States. This fear led to the creation of ARPA and, indirectly, ARPANET - the ancestor of the Internet - to maintain decentralized communications in the event of a nuclear attack.

A crystallographer whose Photo 51 (an X-ray diffraction image of DNA) was passed to Watson and Crick without her consent. She had understood the helical structure, but the data was "borrowed" from her. Having died in 1958, she could not receive the 1962 Nobel Prize.

The process by which the double helix unwinds and each strand serves as a template for the synthesis of a complementary strand. This mechanism ensures the faithful transmission of genetic information during each cell division.

An American dentist who performed the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia in 1846. He attempted to patent it under a code name, but the process was too simple - it spread freely throughout the World in a few months.

Even before anesthesia, post-operative infections were killing patients. Semmelweis (1847) then Lister (1867) imposed hygiene: hand washing, sterilized instruments. These two revolutions - anesthesia and antisepsis - transformed surgery.

A naturalist who independently developed a Theory identical to Darwin's in 1858. His letter precipitated the publication of On the Origin of Species. Their joint presentation to the Linnean Society established their shared priority - Wallace is often forgotten.

Darwinian mechanism: individuals carrying advantageous variations survive and reproduce better, passing these traits to their offspring. Over millennia, this process creates adaptations and new species.

Fossil radiation emitted 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled sufficiently. Detected by Penzias and Wilson in 1965 (Nobel 1978), it is one of the most direct proofs of the Big Bang - a sort of "echo" of the birth of the universe.

Terme: The accelerated expansion of the universe
Explication: Discovered in 1998, the expansion of the universe is accelerating instead of slowing down. This acceleration is attributed to "dark energy" (68% of the total content of the universe), which remains completely misunderstood by current physics.
Theory established in the 1960s: the Earth's surface is divided into rigid plates that move. Volcanoes form at plate boundaries (subduction zones, ridges) or above hotspots like Hawaii.

Process by which an oceanic plate sinks beneath a lighter continental plate. As it descends, it melts and generates magma that rises to the surface. The Pacific "Ring of Fire" results from subduction all around the ocean.

A 1,300 km fault running through California: the Pacific plate slides northwest relative to the North American plate at 6 cm/year. Los Angeles is moving closer to San Francisco - they will be neighbors in 15 million years.
Logarithmic measurement of the energy released by an earthquake. Each degree represents 31.6 times more energy: a magnitude 8 earthquake releases 1,000 times more energy than a 6.

Water-cooled and graphite-moderated nuclear reactor. Its design included a fatal flaw: at low power, it became unstable and could run away. This flaw, known to Soviet engineers, was concealed for ideological reasons.

Area evacuated in an emergency after the accident. Paradoxically, 40 years later, it has become one of the most important nature reserves in Europe: the total absence of human activity benefits wildlife despite residual contamination.

Nom du cours: Why doesn't the Moon fall onto Earth?
Explication: Every mass attracts every other mass, with a force inversely proportional to the square of the distance. The same force explains the falling of the apple and the Moon's orbit - Newton unified terrestrial and celestial physics for the first time.

Nom du cours: Why doesn't the Moon fall onto Earth?
Explication: Since lunar gravity is stronger on the side of the Earth facing it, it creates ocean tides. Conversely, the Earth has slowed the Moon's rotation until synchronization occurred - which is why we always see the same face of the Moon.

Nom du cours: Is there life elsewhere in the Universe?
Explication: Region around a star where the temperature allows water to exist in liquid form on the surface of a planet. Neither too close nor too far - "just like Goldilocks". Our solar system has three potential planets: Venus, Earth, Mars.

Nom du cours: Is there life elsewhere in the Universe?
Explication: Probabilistic formula by Frank Drake (1961) to estimate the number of communicating civilizations in our galaxy. It multiplies factors (stars, habitable planets, duration of civilizations...) - all very uncertain values, making the equation more philosophical than scientific.
The "boundary" of a black hole beyond which nothing can return, not even light. It is not a physical surface but a mathematical limit: the speed required to escape exceeds that of light.

Point at the center of a black hole where density theoretically becomes infinite. The equations of known physics cease to function there - a quantum theory of gravity (not yet developed) would be necessary to describe what happens there.

Nom du cours: The theory of relativity for everyone
Explication: Equivalence between mass and energy: a small mass corresponds to an enormous energy, amplified by the square of the speed of light (300,000 km/s). This is the principle behind the atomic bomb and nuclear energy.

Nom du cours: The theory of relativity for everyone
Explication: Time flows more slowly for an Object in rapid Movement or in an intense gravitational field. GPS systems correct for this time dilation (45 microseconds/day) - without this correction, their accuracy would degrade by 11 km per day.

In storm clouds, updrafts push ice crystals upward and heavy droplets downward. Their friction creates a potential difference of 100 to 300 million volts between the bottom of the cloud and the ground.

For lightning to form, the electric field must be intense enough to strip electrons from air molecules, making it conductive. This channel forms in a few microseconds, heated to 30,000°C - five times the surface of the Sun.
White blood cells that produce antibodies - proteins capable of recognizing and neutralizing a specific pathogen. After vaccination, some become "memory cells" that sometimes persist for a lifetime.

When a sufficient proportion of the population is immunized, the pathogen can no longer spread and indirectly protects non-immunized people. The threshold varies from 80% to 95% depending on the disease.

Gases that absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and re-emit it, warming the atmosphere. The main ones are: water vapor (natural), CO₂, methane (CH₄, 80x more powerful than CO₂ over 20 years), and N₂O.

The ability of a surface to reflect solar radiation. Ice and snow have a high Albedo (reflect a lot), whereas oceans have a low Albedo (absorb more). The melting of ice reduces the global terrestrial albedo, accelerating warming.

A network of brain channels that opens during deep sleep to drain metabolic waste from the brain, notably beta-amyloid proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. Chronic lack of sleep is correlated with an increased risk of dementia.

An internal 24-hour clock regulated by the brain's suprachiasmatic nucleus. Melatonin, produced at night, signals that it is time to sleep. Artificial night light disrupts this rhythm and degrades sleep quality.

Nom du cours: How does the brain store memories?
Explication: The lasting strengthening of synapses between neurons that activate together: "neurons that fire together, wire together". This is the molecular mechanism of learning, notably involving the NMDA receptor.

Nom du cours: How does the brain store memories?
Explication: A form of automatic memory that allows for the learning of gestures and motor skills without a conscious effort of recall.

Repeated DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes, which shorten with each cell division. When they become too short, the cell stops dividing and dies. Telomerase can lengthen them - cancer cells use it to make themselves "immortal".

A tiny jellyfish capable of returning to its juvenile polyp stage after the adult stage - and starting over indefinitely. This process of cellular transdifferentiation is unique and inspires research on cellular reprogramming.
A green pigment contained in chloroplasts. It absorbs red and blue light (reflecting green, hence the color of plants) to power the light-dependent phase of photosynthesis.

The "dark" phase of photosynthesis, occurring in the stroma of chloroplasts. It uses the ATP produced during the light phase to reduce atmospheric CO₂ into glucose - the central reaction of plant nutrition.

Red and purple pigments synthesized in the autumn in leaves. Unlike the carotenoids already present, anthocyanins are newly produced. Their probable role: to protect the leaf during nutrient recovery before it falls.

A layer of cells that forms at the base of the petiole in autumn, blocking the circulation of nutrients. In response to the shortening of days, it develops progressively until it causes the leaf to fall.

A measurement of the speed of stars at different distances from the center. According to Newton, peripheral stars should rotate more slowly. However, they rotate at the same speed - evidence of an invisible mass "gluing" the stars together.

A mysterious force responsible for the acceleration of the expansion of the universe, representing 68% of its total content. Distinct from dark matter (27%), it acts as a repulsive energy of the vacuum, which is still completely misunderstood.

Nom du cours: How does electricity work in our bodies?
Explication: An all-or-nothing electrical signal triggered when the depolarization of a neuron exceeds a threshold. It propagates along the axon at 1 to 100 m/s depending on myelination. It is the "click" of information that the neuron sends.

Nom du cours: How does electricity work in our bodies?
Explication: Chemical molecules released in the synapse that transmit the signal between neurons. The main ones: glutamate (excitatory), GABA (inhibitory), dopamine, serotonin. Psychoactive drugs act on these systems.

Nom du cours: Why do certain sounds give us chills?
Explication: Key mechanism of chills: the brain constantly anticipates the continuation of a melody. When this expectation is violated in a satisfying way (unexpected chord, sudden surge), an emotional release occurs.

Nom du cours: Why do certain sounds give us chills?
Explication: A personality trait associated with curiosity and the appreciation of beauty. People who are highly "open" have an auditory cortex more connected to emotional areas and are significantly more likely to experience musical chills.

Nom du cours: Why do seasons exist on other planets?
Explication: Uranus's axis is almost lying flat on its orbital plane. Each pole receives about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of total darkness - extreme and very long-lasting seasons, with no equivalent in our solar system.

Nom du cours: Why do seasons exist on other planets?
Explication: Mars's orbit is significantly more elliptical than Earth's: the Sun-Mars distance varies from 207 to 249 million km. The Martian southern hemisphere has short, hot summers and long, cold winters - much more pronounced than here.

Were the Iliad and the Odyssey composed by a single poet named Homer or are they the result of a long collective oral tradition? Most researchers today believe in one or two authors who fixed an older tradition.

Terme: The Homeric formula and the oral epic
Explication: The Homeric epics were composed orally before being written. Repeated formulas ("Rosy-fingered Dawn", "Resourceful Odysseus") facilitated memorization and improvised composition - a technique studied by Milman Parry in the 20th century.

Achilles' wrath is not a simple emotion: it is a quasi-cosmic power. The first word of the Iliad, "Mênis", announces this central theme. This divine wrath, which demands reparation, destabilizes the order of the World.

A literary genre of the epic: a long sequence where a hero performs superhuman exploits. Every great warrior of the Iliad has his aristia. These passages allowed for the development of the hero's character and linked his lineage to the gods.

Terme: Fate and free will in Greek tragedy
Explication: Tragedy explores the tension between inevitable fate (predicted by oracles) and human choices. Oedipus fulfills his tragic destiny precisely by trying to flee from it — a paradox at the heart of the human condition according to the Greeks.

Freud borrowed the myth of Oedipus to name the child's unconscious desire for the parent of the opposite sex. This central psychoanalytic concept has very little to do with the reflection of Sophocles, which dealt with fate and free will.

A tension at the heart of Antigone: divine and moral law (burying the dead) against the human law of Creon. This conflict runs through all of political philosophy, from Plato to Rousseau and the theorists of modern natural rights.

Hybris (excess, excessive pride) is the Greek tragic sin par excellence. Creon commits hybris by believing that his law takes precedence over that of the gods — he will lose everything he loved as punishment for this presumption.

Plato distinguishes between physical love and spiritual love aspiring to absolute Beauty. Diotima's speech describes a "ladder of love": starting from a beautiful body, then loving the beauty of souls, then ideal Beauty-in-itself.

A Greek masculine banquet following dinner, combining the consumption of diluted wine and intellectual discussions. Respectable women were excluded from it. It was within this framework that much of Athenian philosophy developed.

Sensible realities are imperfect copies of perfect and eternal Forms. Philosophy is the effort to contemplate these Forms. The allegory of the cave illustrates this fundamental distinction between appearances and true reality.

Only the philosopher — the one who has contemplated the Form of the Good — is fit to rule, according to Plato. His ideal city is a radical intellectual meritocracy, very far from the Athenian democracy that he deeply despised.

Socrates' method of teaching through interrogation: asking questions to lead the interlocutor to discover the truth for themselves. Socrates compared himself to a midwife who helps to "give birth" to ideas already latent in the mind.

The Oracle of Delphi declared that Socrates was the wisest of the Athenians. Socrates concluded that this was because he alone knows that he knows nothing, while others believe they know without having verified it. This humility founds all philosophical pursuit.

A key term for Aristotle: tragedy provokes pity and terror which achieve a "purification" of these emotions in the spectator. A 2,500-year debate: emotional purge, intellectual clarification, or aesthetic pleasure?
For Aristotle, art is an improved imitation (mimesis) of nature — a selective imitation that shows things not as they are but as they could be. Unlike Plato, he sees a positive value in it.

Hesiod describes five successive eras of humanity, each worse than the last: the ages of gold, silver, bronze, heroes, and iron (our own). It is one of the first pessimistic visions of the course of human history.
Hesiod's other great poem, telling the genealogy of the Greek gods from the original Chaos. These two works, along with Homer, constitute the founding texts of Greek religion and mythology.

Terme: The figure of the stranger in Greek tragedy
Explication: Medea is a barbarian (from Colchis), a sorceress, a woman — a triple otherness in the Greek city. Euripides uses this external figure to criticize Athenian values regarding women, marriage, and the Law.

Terme: Revenge and honor in the Greek world
Explication: Honor (timē) was a fundamental value in Greece. Betrayal demanded reparation. Medea cannot accept the dishonor of being repudiated: her revenge follows a logic of reciprocity which, pushed to the extreme, becomes monstrous.

Terme: The penal colonies and the penal system in the 19th century
Explication: The penal colonies of Toulon, Brest, and Rochefort were places of forced labor where convicts suffered dehumanizing living conditions, illustrating the severity of a justice system that criminalized poverty.

An incorruptible and legalistic policeman who hunts Valjean throughout his life. Born in prison to a prostitute mother, he has made the Law his only religion. He represents the blind rigor of a justice without mercy or the possibility of redemption.
A state of chronic dissatisfaction born from the disproportion between dreams nourished by the imagination (reading, fantasies) and lived reality.
A narrative Technique allowing the reporting of a Figure's words or thoughts in the indirect style but without an introductory verb, creating a confusion between the narrator and the Figure.

Nom du cours: The Red and the Black, Stendhal
Terme: The symbolism of The Red and the Black
Explication: Debated since 1830: red would symbolize the Napoleonic army (the path of success) and black the priestly robe (the Other path under the Restoration). Julien Sorel navigates between these two paths - neither truly suits him.

Nom du cours: The Red and the Black, Stendhal
Explication: A Period where the Bourbons were restored to the throne after Waterloo. Society was dominated by the nobility and the Church, hostile to revolutionary values. Stendhal saw it as a society of hypocrisy and provincial mediocrity.

Philosophy according to which God created the best of all possible worlds and that apparent evil serves a higher good. Voltaire wrote Candide in response, notably to the Lisbon earthquake (1755) which killed 60,000 people in a few minutes.

18th-century intellectual Movement based on reason, the critique of prejudice, and progress. Voltaire, Rousseau, Diderot, Hume, and Kant questioned religious and Politics authority - intellectually paving the way for future revolutions.
Rousseau postulated that man is naturally good and that it is society that corrupts him. This idea, opposed to Hobbes, deeply influenced the French Revolution and romanticism.

Woman from the Savoyard nobility who welcomed the young Rousseau at age 16, converted him to Catholicism, and became his protectress and then his mistress. Rousseau calls her "Maman" in The Confessions, mixing filial affection and a romantic relationship.

A feeling born from the clash between the human desire for meaning and the silence of the universe. Camus does not see the absurd as a cosmic truth but as a lived experience - the response is not suicide but lucid and conscious revolt.

The Stranger takes place in French Algeria during the 1940s. The Arab whom Meursault kills remains nameless in the novel - a major postcolonial critique: the novel is said to reproduce the invisibility of Arabs in French colonial Literature.
An attitude of living to the peak of one's consciousness while refusing any hope of transcendent meaning, thus transforming finitude into freedom.

Camus critiques the "leap" that some philosophers take when faced with the absurd: leaping into faith (Kierkegaard) or revolutionary hope (Marx). These "philosophical suicides" avoid the absurd instead of confronting it honestly.

Nom du cours: In Search of Lost Time, Proust
Explication: A memory suddenly triggered by a sensation (taste, smell) resurrects a lived past in its emotional entirety, unlike voluntary memory, which is cold and intellectual. The madeleine is the canonical example.

Nom du cours: In Search of Lost Time, Proust
Explication: In the final volume, the narrator understands that only art can snatch lived moments from the destruction of time. Literature can restore the past - this is the justification for the entire Recherche and its final revelation.

A project of 90 interconnected novels and short stories describing the whole of French society. Characters return from one novel to another - an innovation unheard of at the time. Rastignac appears in about twenty works of the cycle.

An escaped convict and criminal genius, he is the cynical mentor to Rastignac. A recurring figure in the Comédie humaine, he represents out-of-law society - powerful, lucid and without illusions about the respectable world.

Baudelaire is the father of symbolism: he sought not to describe reality but to suggest secret correspondences between sensations, emotions and ideas. Verlaine, Rimbaud and Mallarmé, then the entire Poetics of the 20th century, claim his heritage.

Cosmic boredom, a feeling of the futility of the world, an inability to find meaning or joy - faced with an inaccessible ideal. Spleen and ideal are the two opposing poles between which all the poetry of Les Fleurs du Mal oscillates.

The official language of Oceania whose objective is to make dissident thought impossible by eliminating the words that would allow it to be formulated. The more the vocabulary is reduced, the more complex ideas become unthinkable.

Orwell had observed Stalinism in Spain during the Civil War and experienced the Blitz in London. 1984 is inspired by Staline but embodies a universal totalitarianism: the claim to control not only bodies but reality itself ("2+2=5").

Terme: The allegory of the Russian Revolution
Explication: Old Major = Marx/Lenin, Napoleon = Stalin, Snowball = Trotsky, Squealer = propaganda. The commands, progressively modified, illustrate the betrayal of revolutionary ideals by the bureaucracy in power.

Soviet regime under Stalin (1924-1953): cult of personality, political terror (Gulag, Great Purges), planned economy, forced collectivization. The Farm was written in 1943-1944, while the USSR was an ally of Great Britain.

Revenge is a central theme of Elizabethan theater. A man of honor had to avenge an offense to his family - but this duty conflicted with the Law and Christian morality. This paradox fuels Hamlet's fundamental hesitation.

In Shakespeare's time, melancholy was a medical "humor" (black bile) associated with people of intellect, creativity, and inaction. Hamlet's hesitation corresponds to this medical diagnosis of the period, which explains his inability to act.

A literary tradition glorifying the secret and suffering love of a knight for a lady (often married). Romeo begins the play in this stereotypical role (in love with Rosalind) before his love for Juliet becomes real and tragic.

Terme: The Italian source of the narrative
Explication: Romeo and Juliet is based on a novella by Matteo Bandello (1554), itself inspired by earlier tales. Shakespeare adapted it by tightening the timeframe (from months to a few days) to intensify the tragedy's fatality.

Methods of industrial organization that rationalized production through the extreme division of tasks and the assembly line. Huxley applies them to human reproduction and conditioning - Ford is the deity of the novel.

Fictional drug in the novel that brings happiness and oblivion without side effects. It symbolizes all forms of chemical or technological addiction allowing individuals to endure a meaningless existence—foreshadowing social media.

Subtitle of the novel: "The Modern Prometheus". Victor Frankenstein creates something extraordinary without accepting the consequences. The real monster may not be the creature but its creator who abandons it at birth.

The eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815 projected ash that darkened the global atmosphere, causing a freezing summer in Europe in 1816. In this apocalyptic context, Mary Shelley (18 years old) wrote Frankenstein during a stay on the shores of Lake Geneva.

Intellectual movement rejecting all moral and religious authority in the name of reason and science. Real-life nihilists assassinated Tsar Alexander II in 1881. Raskolnikov embodies a tragic and individualized version of this ideology.

Central theme in Dostoyevsky: it is accepted suffering and voluntary humiliation that purify the soul. Raskolnikov will heal not through reason but through humiliating confession and the love of Sonia, a figure of Christ-like sacrifice.

Adjective that has entered every language to describe an absurd bureaucratic situation where an individual is crushed by an impersonal and incomprehensible system, with no possible recourse. It often precedes the knowledge of the novel itself.

Josef K. is perhaps guilty simply of existing, in a world whose rules are incomprehensible. This existential reading of Kafka influenced Sartre and Camus in their own explorations of the human condition.

Don Quixote is one of the first novels to comment on itself: in the second part (1615), the figures have read the first part (1605) and discuss it. This game with the reality of the novel anticipates literary postmodernism by several centuries.

Terme: The Battle of Lepanto (1571) and Cervantes' captivity
Explication: Cervantes fought at the Battle of Lepanto and was wounded (losing the use of his left hand). Captured by pirates in 1575, he was an enslaved person in Algiers for five years. These experiences forged the writer and nourish the humor and depth of the novel.

Agricultural disaster in the Great Plains caused by drought and destructive farming practices. Dust storms blackened the sky as far as New York, forcing hundreds of thousands of families (the "Okies") to migrate to California.

Terme: The American labor movement of the 1930s
Explication: The Great Depression radicalized American workers: the rise of the CIO, massive strikes, socialism. Steinbeck's novel is part of this context of social struggle that influenced Roosevelt's New Deal.

Nom du cours: To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee
Terme: Jim Crow laws and the segregated South
Explication: Jim Crow laws (1877-1965) organized segregation in the South. A Black man accused by a white woman was practically condemned in advance by all-white juries — a central reality of justice in the novel.

Nom du cours: To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee
Explication: Fictional lawyer who became the archetype of American moral integrity. His defense of Tom Robinson, whom he knows is innocent but cannot save, illustrates the tragedy of a society where law and justice do not coincide.

Terme: The American Dream and its corruption
Explication: The novel is the most famous critique of the American Dream: the idea that one can rise through merit alone. Gatsby succeeds but discovers that social class and the past are insurmountable — old money despises the nouveau riche.

Constitutional ban on the manufacture and sale of alcohol. It gave rise to organized crime and allowed men like Gatsby to make a fortune quickly via bootlegging — the glittering facade of a morally corrupt era.

Nom du cours: The Lord of the Rings, Tolkien
Explication: Tolkien developed the Concept of "sub-creation": the writer creates a secondary World with its own laws and internal coherence. The reader enters it through "secondary belief" - the voluntary suspension of disbelief. Tolkien saw it as a quasi-divine act.

Nom du cours: The Lord of the Rings, Tolkien
Explication: Tolkien, a professor of Old English at Oxford, was deeply inspired by Beowulf, the Norse Edda, and the Finnish Kalevala. His avowed goal: to create a Mythology for England, which did not possess one like Greece or Scandinavia.

A Period of anti-communist witch hunts. Artists and writers were blacklisted. Bradbury was concerned about Censorship through fear, social and politics pressure on thought - much more than through the books themselves.

Terme: The entertainment society and fragmented attention
Explication: Bradbury anticipated self-censorship through entertainment: people so saturated with fast media that they no longer wish to read. The "parlors" (wall-screens) in the novel anticipate television and later smartphones.

Nom du cours: One Hundred Years of Solitude, García Márquez
Explication: A literary style that presents magical events with the same naturalness as real events, without surprise or explanation. Emerging from a Latin American tradition where the marvelous is part of daily life.

Nom du cours: One Hundred Years of Solitude, García Márquez
Terme: The United Fruit Company and the "banana republics"
Explication: The banana company in the novel refers to the American United Fruit Company which economically dominated several Central American countries. A massacre of striking workers that it caused inspired a key scene in the novel.

An intellectual Movement centering reflection on the human being, drawing inspiration from rediscovered Greek and Roman texts. Humanists (Petrarch, Erasmus) valued liberal education, human dignity, and the development of individual faculties.

A Technique developed by Brunelleschi around 1415: parallel lines converge toward a vanishing point, creating an illusion of depth on a flat surface. This revolution in gaze radically distinguishes Renaissance painting from medieval Art.
Annual exhibition of the Academy of Fine Arts, the only showcase for art in France in the 19th century. Being rejected meant commercial invisibility.

Terme: Paint tubes and the plein air
Explication: The invention of metal paint tubes (1841) allowed painters to work outdoors. Without the tubes, paint oxidized quickly. This banal Technique innovation was a material condition for the impressionist revolution.
17th-century artistic style characterized by Movement, dramatic contrast, theatricality, and a strong emotional charge aiming to impress the viewer.
Major Italian painter (1593-1656), follower of Caravaggism, famous for her scenes of strength and female vengeance with striking realism.

In the 17th century, the United Provinces became the world's leading commercial power. This prosperity created a wealthy Protestant middle class that wanted portraits, genre scenes, and landscapes - a market that allowed Rembrandt and Vermeer to exist.

Rembrandt went bankrupt at the height of his reputation, after spending lavishly on Art collections. His possessions were sold at auction. This ruin forced him to paint under the names of his wife Hendrickje and his son Titus.

Terme: African and Oceanic art as influence
Explication: Picasso's discovery of African masks around 1906-1907 was a revelation: an art that did not seek to imitate reality but to provide a symbolic and structural representation of it. Decisive for the Demoiselles d'Avignon.

Innovation of synthetic Cubism (1912): Braque and Picasso pasted pieces of newspapers and wallpaper into their paintings. By integrating fragments of reality into the work of art, they blurred the boundary between representation and reality.

Surrealism was directly inspired by Freud: the unconscious as a reservoir of repressed images, dreams as the royal road to the unconscious, free association. André Breton had met Freud in 1921 and wanted to liberate the unconscious in art.

Surrealist Technique: writing or painting without conscious control, letting the flow of the unconscious express itself directly. Breton used it as a Poetics tool. Dalí developed his own pictorial variant with the paranoiac-critical method.

Terme: German Expressionism (Die Brücke, Der Blaue Reiter)
Explication: German artistic movements (1905-1920) pushing expressionism to the extreme: radical deformation of forms, garish colors, distressing themes. Kirchner, Kandinsky, Nolde were reacting to modernization and foreshadowing the trauma of 1914.

Terme: The eruption of Krakatoa (1883) and the red sky
Explication: The catastrophic eruption of Krakatoa projected ash that colored sunsets blood-red around the World for months. Munch noted in his diary having seen a sky of "blood and fire" — likely this phenomenon.

Terme: The Bauhaus and the art-industry synthesis
Explication: School of Art and design founded in Weimar in 1919 which attempted to reconcile the major arts and applied arts. Kandinsky and Klee taught there. Its minimalist and functional aesthetic is omnipresent in contemporary design.

Dutch movement founded in 1917: reducing art to its purest elements - horizontal and vertical lines, primary colors, white and black. Mondrian sought a universal visual language beyond any specific culture.

After the war, the American economy produced unprecedented abundance. Advertising and mass media created a culture of standardized images that Pop Art used as artistic material, questioning the boundary between art and product.

Terme: The aura and mechanical reproduction (Walter Benjamin)
Explication: Benjamin (1935) analyzed how technical reproduction destroys the "aura" of the unique work. Warhol radicalized this idea: by mechanically reproducing popular images, he questioned the very notion of original and author.

First electronic instrument (1920), played without physical contact: two antennas detect the position of the hands and control pitch and volume. Its ethereal sound was used in 1950s horror films and by the Beach Boys.

Chicago house (1984) used drum machines and deep bass. Detroit techno (1986-1988) was colder and more mechanical. Both emerged from marginalized Black and Latino communities and became global phenomena.

Rediscovery of traditional American music by urban artists in the 1950s-60s. Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie made folk the soundtrack of the labor and civil rights movements. Dylan was its prodigal heir.

In the Guthrie tradition, protest folk used accessible melodies to spread political messages. Dylan's "Blowin' in the Wind" and "The Times They Are A-Changin'" became anthems of the Civil Rights Movement.

New York urban planner who built urban highways devastating working-class neighborhoods in the Bronx during the 1950s-60s. The Cross-Bronx Expressway destroyed 60,000 housing units, creating the conditions of dereliction in which hip-hop was born.

Technique consisting of using extracts from existing records as the basis for a new Work. Legally problematic, sampling was recognized as a form of legitimate artistic creation after long legal battles.

Movement for Italy's national reunification (circa 1815-1871). Verdi's operas - notably "Va, pensiero" from Nabucco - became nationalist anthems. Verdi himself was a symbol: his name was used as an acronym for Vittorio Emanuele, Re D'Italia.

Two Italian genres: opera seria (noble subjects, tragedy) and opera buffa (comic subjects, ordinary characters). Verdi excelled in opera seria but renewed the genres by integrating realistic psychological drama and social tension.

Nom du cours: Mozart: child prodigy and tragic life
Terme: The status of the musician in the 18th century
Explication: Social status where the musician is considered a servant attached to a nobleman or a prelate, having to compose and play according to the desires of his patron.

Nom du cours: Mozart: child prodigy and tragic life
Explication: The Magic Flute (1791) is a masonic allegory: Tamino's initiatory trials, the struggle between light/darkness reflect the masonic rituals and ideals of the Enlightenment to which Mozart had adhered since 1784.

Absolute music (Beethoven) expresses pure emotions without external reference. Program music (Berlioz, Liszt) tells a story. This distinction structures the great aesthetic debate of the romantic 19th century.

Terme: The Ode to Joy and the European anthem
Explication: The last Movement of the 9th Symphony, based on Schiller's poem, became the official anthem of the European Union in 1985. The universalism of its message (brotherhood of humanity) makes it the symbol of the European ideal of unity.

Terme: Segregation in the American music industry
Explication: American radio stations in the 1940s and 50s refused to broadcast "race music" (blues, R&B) on "white" stations. The birth of rock'n'roll occurred largely when white artists covered Black styles, raising questions of cultural appropriation.
A 1940s genre combining electrified blues, jazz, and gospel, created by Black artists. Rhythm and blues was the direct foundation of rock'n'roll: Elvis and Chuck Berry were directly inspired by it.

Counterpoint is the art of combining several independent melodies according to harmonic rules. The fugue is its most elaborate form: a theme is presented by different voices in turn, then developed in increasingly complex combinations.

Bach's "Well-Tempered Clavier" (48 preludes and fugues in all keys) demonstrated that a uniform tuning allowed playing in all keys without sounding out of tune. This system is the one used by all modern instruments.

Place where Louisiana law allowed enslaved people to gather on Sundays to play and dance. This unique location in North America allowed for the preservation of African musical traditions which, combined with European harmony, gave birth to jazz.

Unlike classical music, jazz makes improvisation its heart: the musician invents their melodic line in real time, over an agreed-upon harmonic grid, in response to others. It is both total freedom and a demanding discipline.

Nom du cours: The blues: roots of all modern music
Explication: The founding harmonic architecture of the blues: a sequence of 12-bar in three parts (tonic, subdominant, dominant) that repeats. This infinitely variable structure is the grid upon which the blues is improvised and is found in rock, jazz, and pop.

Nom du cours: The blues: roots of all modern music
Explication: "Bent" notes between two notes of the standard scale, played slightly below their usual pitch. These microtonal inflections come from the African vocal tradition and give blues its specific expressive and poignant character.

Photographic process on paper (circa 1840) allowing for several prints to be made from a negative - unlike the unique daguerreotype. It is the direct ancestor of film photography used until the digital age.

Terme: The impact of photography on figurative painting
Explication: Photography freed painting from its documentary function. Painters no longer had to immortalization faces or battles - photography did it better and for less. This liberation is one of the conditions for impressionism and then abstraction.

Terme: The Lumière brothers and early cinema
Explication: Cinema was born in France (Enlightenment, 1895) but became industrialized in the United States. Hollywood established itself in the 1910s-1920s thanks to the Californian sun, the diversity of landscapes, and the massive immigration of European talent.

A comic genre of silent cinema based on physical gags, falls, chases, and grotesque violence. The term comes from a theater prop. Charlot brought this genre to its perfection by adding emotional depth and social criticism.
Cinematographic technique where all planes of the image (foreground, middle ground, background) are sharp simultaneously, allowing for complex action within a single frame.
American press tycoon of the early 20th century whose life served as a model for the figure of Charles Foster Kane.

Theory by Truffaut in the Cahiers du Cinéma (1954): the true author of a film is the director, who expresses his personal vision. It promoted Hollywood filmmakers like Hitchcock or Hawks whom French academic critics despised.

Terme: Shooting on location and the lightweight camera
Explication: The Nouvelle Vague technically reinvented cinema: lightweight portable cameras, fast film stocks allowing filming without artificial lighting. These budgetary constraints became a revolutionary aesthetic - cinema "taken to the streets".

British science fiction author who co-wrote the screenplay for 2001 from the short story "The Sentinel" (1948). He invented the concept of the geostationary communication satellite in 1945 - long before its technical realization.

HAL 9000 is one of the first depictions of a conscious AI in conflict with its creators. Its anthropomorphism (calm voice, relentless logic, self-preservation) foreshadows current debates on AI safety.

Hitchcock's term for the object that all characters pursue (the suitcase, the secret plans) but whose content has no importance for the viewer. What matters is the desire it arouses and the narrative dynamics it generates.

Technique where the camera adopts the point of view of a character, making the viewer experience exactly what they see. In Vertigo, Scottie's vertigo is transmitted by a zoom-out/dolly-in technique invented for the film.

Terme: The flying buttress and the rib vault
Explication: Structural innovations of Gothic architecture. The rib vault distributes weight onto ribs rather than the entire walls. The flying buttress transfers the thrust outwards, allowing walls to be opened into windows without the building collapsing.

Suger theorized that divine light, channeled through colored stained glass, elevated the soul toward God. This "metaphysics of light" inspired Gothic architecture in its pursuit of ever larger windows and ever higher arches.

Principle of The Bauhaus: form follows function. A well-designed Object is beautiful because it perfectly fulfills its use - without superfluous ornamentation. This principle structures modern industrial design.

Hitler closed The Bauhaus in 1933, considering its aesthetics as "degenerate". Its teachers emigrated to the United States (Gropius to Harvard, Mies van der Rohe to Chicago), where they profoundly influenced American architecture and design.

Technique by Leonardo da Vinci: very thin layers of translucent glaze (sometimes 40 layers) create imperceptible transitions between light and shadow. It is this sfumato that makes the smile of The Mona Lisa so ambiguous and elusive.

Terme: The theft of the Mona Lisa (1911)
Explication: Vincenzo Peruggia, a Louvre employee, stole The Mona Lisa and kept it at his home in Florence for two years. This theft made headlines around the World and transformed The Mona Lisa, then little known to the general public, into the most famous painting in the World.
Central Concept for Van Gogh where the Work does not seek to reproduce physical reality but the painter's emotions and visions.

Van Gogh invited Gauguin to share his yellow house in Arles. After two months of difficult coexistence, a violent argument precipitated Van Gogh's crisis, who cut off his ear and was voluntarily institutionalized in Saint-Rémy.
Conflict between the Spanish Republic and the Francoist uprising supported by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. Spain was the testing ground for the new bombing tactics of the coming Second World War.
Air military unit of the Luftwaffe sent to Spain to support Franco and test new saturation bombing tactics. The bombing of Guernica was its first massive use against a civilian city.
Three revolutionary days that overthrew King Charles X, who wanted to suppress freedom of the press and reduce voting rights. Louis Philippe I took the constitutional throne in his place.

An allegorical female figure embodying the French Republic since the Revolution. Her Phrygian cap (a symbol of ancient freedom) is her distinctive attribute. Delacroix's Liberty is its founding image, reproduced in every town hall in France.

Painting done on fresh plaster (fresco = fresh in Italian). The pigments integrate into the plaster as it dries, making the color permanent and resistant over centuries. Michelangelo had to work in daily sections (giornata) on his back from a scaffold.

Theory by Frank Meshberger (1990): the shape of the red cloak surrounding God is said to exactly reproduce the anatomical cross-section of a human brain. If intentional, Michelangelo would have symbolized that God is a creation of the human mind.

Terme: Louis Leroy and the birth of the term "impressionism"
Explication: An art critic for "Le Charivari", Louis Leroy wrote a sarcastic article in 1874: "Impression, I was certain of it!". He intended to mock — the term "impressionists" was adopted by the artists themselves with pride, turning the insult around.

Terme: The industrialized port of Le Havre in the 19th century
Explication: Le Havre was the leading French commercial port, transformed by industrialization. Monet shows precisely this industrial modernity (steam, cranes, small boats) in the morning mist — a fleeting vision of modernity in progress.

Nighthawks was painted in 1942, a few weeks after Pearl Harbor. The isolation of the characters in the American night reflects a profound unease: the individualism of American society, the lack of community, the emptiness behind material abundance.

Cultural Institution: restaurant open 24/7, fast counter service, anonymous passing clientele. An ultimate Place of collective solitude, it feeds the iconography of American literature, cinema (film noir), and painting.

An early 20th-century trend seeking a lost vitality in African and Oceanic arts. Picasso found there a radical freedom of representation that broke the conventions of perspective held since the Renaissance.
