A dilapidated building in Montmartre where Picasso lived and worked from 1904 to 1909, surrounded by artists and poets (Max Jacob, Apollinaire, Braque). It was there, in a studio without water or heating, that he painted the Demoiselles d'Avignon.

Bergson distinguished between physical time (measurable) and lived time (subjective, elastic). Dalí's soft watches visually illustrate this "Bergsonian time": in dreams, time expands, contracts, and loses all rigidity.

A rocky coastal landscape of the Costa Brava visible in many of Dalí's paintings. The characteristic eroded granite geological formations of this cape fueled his imagination for ambiguous and melting forms.

A group of 12 to 15 citizens who sing, dance, and comment on the action between episodes. The chorus represents the voice of the community and provides a moral perspective on the heroes' actions. Its role gradually diminished under Sophocles and Euripides.

An ancient theater from the 4th century BC, capable of seating 14,000 spectators. Its extraordinary acoustics (a coin drop can be heard from any seat) remain mysterious and surpass the capabilities of modern acoustic engineering.

A theater built on the south bank of the Thames, outside the limits of the City of London (which banned performances). Octagonal and open to the sky, it hosted 3,000 spectators standing (the "groundlings") or seated in the covered galleries.
Unrhymed 10-syllable line (iambic pentameter) used by Shakespeare for noble Figures. Commoners spoke in prose. This social distinction through language is a convention of Elizabethan theater.

Nom du cours: Freedom of the press and photojournalism
Explication: Fundamental tension: how far should a photographer get involved? Kevin Carter photographed a vulture waiting for a Sudanese child to die (1993) and was accused of not helping. He received the Pulitzer then committed suicide three months later.

Nom du cours: Freedom of the press and photojournalism
Explication: French photographer, founder of the Magnum agency (1947) and theorist of the "decisive moment": the unique instant where form and content coincide perfectly. His Work with the Leica is considered the pinnacle of humanist photojournalism.

Nom du cours: The birth of the Greek gods (Cronus, Zeus, Olympus)
Explication: Poem (circa 700 BC) recounting the origin and genealogy of the Greek gods since Chaos. Our main source on Greek cosmogony, it presents passionate and violent gods, subjected like men to the forces of destiny.

Nom du cours: The birth of the Greek gods (Cronus, Zeus, Olympus)
Explication: Greek gods are entirely human in their emotions (jealousy, love, anger) but immortal and supernatural. Xenophanes already criticized this vision: "if horses had gods, they would represent them as horses".

Terme: The Promethean myth in modern culture
Explication: Prometheus has become the symbol of human emancipation through knowledge, defying the limits set by the gods. Goethe, Shelley (Frankenstein), Marx claimed him as a symbol - he embodies the modernity rebelling against the established order.

His name means "the one who thinks after". He accepted without thinking Pandora's gift sent by Zeus. His recklessness introduced evils into the World. The Prometheus-Epimetheus pair illustrates the opposition between foresight and impulsivity.

The myth of Pandora is often read as a mythological justification for the Greeks' mistrust of women: it is a woman who introduces evil into the World, through curiosity or disobedience. A myth parallel to Eve in the Bible.

In Hesiod's version, Hope remains in the jar when Pandora closes it. A fundamental ambiguity: is it the last benevolent gift of the gods, or an additional evil (false hope, illusion) that tortures men by making them believe that things will improve?

Secret initiation ceremonies celebrated at Eleusis for over a millennium (600 BC - 400 AD). Based on the myth of Persephone, they promised initiates a blissful life after death. Plato and Marcus Aurelius were initiated into them.

Terme: The agricultural cycle in Greek religion
Explication: The myth of Persephone is a mythological explanation of the vegetative cycle: when she descends into the Underworld (autumn-winter), the earth is sterile; when she ascends (spring), the vegetation is reborn. Greek religion was linked to agricultural rhythms.

Terme: Catabasis: the descent into the Underworld
Explication: A recurring mythological motif: the hero descends into the Underworld alive (Heracles, Odysseus, Aeneas, Orpheus). This "catabasis" symbolizes the initiatory journey into death and the confrontation with the unconscious.

A religious movement inspired by the myth of Orpheus, advocating for the purification of the soul and metempsychosis (transmigration of souls). It influenced Pythagoras and Plato in their conception of the immortality of the soul.

A term coined by Freud (1914): excessive love of oneself, inability to love others. In the myth, Narcissus cannot love Echo because he loves only his own image. Freud distinguished primary narcissism (healthy) from pathological narcissism.

The repercussion of a sound on a surface and its return to its source. The word "echo" comes directly from the nymph in the myth, condemned to only repeat the last words heard. This myth explained the natural acoustic phenomenon to the Greeks.

Icarus embodies classic Hybris: failing to respect human limits and seeking to rise to the gods. This transgression is always punished in Greek mythology - the Greeks saw in hubris the tragic fault par excellence.

Daedalus's construction imprisoning the Minotaur. Beyond the myth, the Labyrinth has become a universal symbol of wandering, of the quest and the impossible return - of the unconscious or of inextricable destiny.

Terme: The absurd in Camus and Sisyphus
Explication: In The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), Camus chooses this myth because Sisyphus knows his fate and continues anyway. Camus concludes that "one must imagine Sisyphus happy" - only the refusal of resignation makes the absurd bearable.

Sisyphus was punished for having cheated death twice and revealed secrets of the gods. In Greek mythology, mortals who defied the divine order or claimed immortality received eternal and exemplary punishments.

Expression describing any situation where what one desires is almost within reach but always inaccessible. This universal symbol of frustration and temptation has crossed all cultures and is found in psychological theories on desire.
Named as such in 1802 by Ekeberg because it is insoluble in acids - like Tantalus who can swallow nothing. It is used in capacitors for smartphones and in biocompatible medical prostheses.

Representation of the head of Medusa used as an Apotropaic amulet (to ward off evil) throughout ancient Greece. It was found on temples, shields, rings, mosaics. It passed into Roman Art and then into medieval coats of arms.

When Perseus decapitates Medusa, the winged horse Pegasus is born from her blood. He would be captured by Bellerophon with the help of Athena and would allow him to defeat the Chimera. Pegasus has become the universal symbol of poetic inspiration.

Greek heroism (Hercules, Achilles) values strength, warrior glory, and prowess - even if Hercules acts out of penance. Christian heroism values humility, sacrifice, and accepted suffering. This tension structures Western culture.

Promontories of Gibraltar that ancient tradition considered the boundaries of the known world. The expression "nec plus ultra" was associated with them. Columbus crossed them in 1492, pushing back the limits of the known World towards the West.

Terme: The Labyrinth of Knossos in Crete
Explication: Excavations at Knossos revealed the Minoan palace, with its complex layout evoking a labyrinth. The Minoan civilization (2700-1450 BC) and its bull cult are likely at the origin of the myth of the Minotaur.

An expression that has entered every language to designate a landmark allowing one to find their way in a complex situation. Ariadne gives Theseus a thread to exit the labyrinth - a symbol of memory, method, and the help of the Other.

Practical intelligence, cunning, the ability to reverse an unfavorable situation. Odysseus embodies metis par excellence - his Homeric epithet is "of many wiles." It is opposed to biē (brute force) embodied by Ajax.

One-eyed beings, sons of Uranus and Gaia: divine blacksmiths who forged the lightning of Zeus. In Homer, Polyphemus and his kind are wild shepherds ignorant of the gods and laws - an embodiment of barbarism.

Region east of the Black Sea, described in Greek myths as the end of the eastern World. Shepherds there used sheep fleeces to filter gold from the gold-bearing rivers of the Caucasus - the "golden fleece" may have been real.

Daughter of the king of Colchis, she betrayed her father and sacrificed her brother for Jason. When Jason abandoned her for a politics alliance in Corinth, her revenge - killing their own children - is the most terrible act in all of Greek Mythology.

Supreme value of heroic culture: immortal glory acquired through warlike exploits and transmitted by poets. Achilles deliberately chooses a short but glorious life over a long life without glory - a fundamental choice of Greek heroic ethics.

Achilles' elite warriors, legendarily created by Zeus from ants (myrmex = ant in Greek). In the Iliad, they are the most feared soldiers. Their absolute loyalty to Achilles illustrates the unbreakable bond between a hero and his men.

Hybrid creature present in many cultures: Egyptian Sphinx (lion, human head, royal symbol) and Greek Sphinx (female, winged, poser of deadly riddles). The same image takes on opposite meanings depending on the culture.

Oedipus's (unintentional) incest represents the ultimate transgression of social order: the confusion of generations. For the Greeks, it caused a defilement (miasma) affecting the entire community, visible in the pestilence striking Thebes.

Nom du cours: Antigone: family duty vs. state law
Explication: Hegel was the first (1807) to theorize that in Antigone, both protagonists are each right according to their own principles - family vs State, divine Law vs human Law. It is not a matter of good and evil but of two incompatible goods: the very definition of the tragic.

Nom du cours: Antigone: family duty vs. state law
Explication: Play performed in Paris under the Nazi Occupation. Anouilh deliberately left its Politics reading ambiguous: Creon could represent the Germans or Vichy, Antigone the Resistance. Both sides found what they were looking for in the Work - genius or opportunism?

Nom du cours: The Trojan War and the wooden horse
Explication: Schliemann located Troy in 1870 at Hisarlik, Turkey. Excavations revealed nine successive cities. Troy VIIa (around 1184 BC) shows traces of fire compatible with the Homeric account - the Trojan War may have actually taken place.

Nom du cours: The Trojan War and the wooden horse
Explication: After the Trojan War, Greek heroes experience tragic returns: Agamemnon is murdered, Ajax dies. Only Menelaus finds Helen again. These "Nostoi" formed an epic cycle (now lost) that was as important as the Iliad for the ancient Greeks.

An Icelandic Poetics and Mythology treatise from the 13th century. Although written in a Christian context, it constitutes the most structured source on Norse beliefs, intended to preserve the Art of ancient poetry.

Thor's hammer was the most widespread symbol of protection in medieval Scandinavia. Linked to a solar symbol (Norse swastika), it was misappropriated by the Nazis in the 20th century - giving this unfortunate symbol a lasting connotation.

Nom du cours: Ragnarök: the end of the Norse world
Explication: Norse cosmic ash tree connecting the nine worlds. Its roots delve into the realms of the gods, the Giants, and the dead. The Norns (weavers of fate) live at its base. The cosmic tree is an almost universal mythological archetype.

Nom du cours: Ragnarök: the end of the Norse world
Explication: The vision of Ragnarök shares traits with other eschatologies: the Christian Last Judgment, the Hindu Kali Yuga. These apocalyptic visions reflect a universal concern for the end of times and, often, the Renaissance that follows.

Fundamental principle of Egyptian thought: cosmic order, truth and justice. The pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma'at against chaos. Osiris presides over the judgment of the dead, weighing their heart against the feather of Ma'at.

A collection of magical spells accompanying deceased Egyptians into the afterlife. It guided the soul through the trials of the underworld, notably the judgment before Osiris. Some illustrated papyri are among the most beautiful Works of Egyptian Art.

A collective term for the civilizations of the Fertile Crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (modern Iraq). They invented cuneiform writing, codified Law (Code of Hammurabi), sexagesimal mathematics and astronomy.

Terme: The Flood narrative in the Epic
Explication: Tablet XI of the Epic contains a universal Flood myth earlier than the biblical Deluge: Utnapishtim builds a boat and brings all the animals on board. This parallel stunned biblical scholars when it was discovered in 1872.

Nom du cours: Romulus and Remus: the founding of Rome
Explication: The traditional Date of the founding of Rome, calculated by Varro in the 1st century BC. The Romans counted years "from the founding of the city" (AUC). This legendary Date corresponded to the monarchy of the seven kings of Rome.

Nom du cours: Romulus and Remus: the founding of Rome
Explication: A bronze statue of a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, symbol of Rome. Long believed to be Etrusque (5th century BC), recent studies date it to the Middle Ages. The human twins were added by Pollaiolo in the 15th century.

Samsara: the cycle of soul reincarnations. Karma: the Law of moral causality - every action has consequences for future lives. Vishnu descends to the World in avatars specifically to restore the disturbed cosmic Karma.

Central philosophical text of Hinduism extracted from the Mahabharata: Krishna (avatar of Vishnu) explains to Arjuna the meaning of duty (dharma) and selfless action before the battle. Admired by Thoreau, Emerson, Gandhi, and Oppenheimer.

Norse warriors sought to die with weapons in hand to be chosen by the Valkyries. Dying of illness ("straw death") did not open the gates of Valhalla - this vision of a warrior paradise structured Viking culture.

Richard Wagner set Norse mythology to music in Der Ring des Nibelungen (1848-1874). "The Ride of the Valkyries" is among the best-known works of classical music in the world, often associated with American cinema.

The Phoenix bird was adopted by alchemists as a symbol of transmutation: as it is reborn from its ashes, base metals can be transformed into gold. Its presence is recurrent in hermetic and esoteric literature.

Chinese mythological bird symbol of virtue and grace, associated with the Empress (as the dragon is with the Emperor). Its reappearance announced a virtuous and just reign. It embodies the five Confucian virtues.

Terme: Order and chaos in Greek mythology
Explication: The Titanomachy represents the victory of Olympian order (Zeus, reason, law) over the primordial chaos of the Titans. This narrative structure - a cosmic struggle between order and chaos - is found in all major world mythologies.

Titan condemned to carry the heavens (and not the Earth, contrary to popular belief) on his shoulders for eternity. His name gave "Atlas" to map collections as early as the 16th century (Mercator illustrated him on the cover).

Nom du cours: Dionysus: the god of wine and excess
Terme: The birth of theater from Dionysus
Explication: Greek tragedies and comedies were born from Dionysian rituals. Thespis (6th century) was the first to introduce an actor distinct from the chorus - the founding act of Western theater. The theater of Athens was itself a place of worship for Dionysus.

Nom du cours: Dionysus: the god of wine and excess
Explication: Philosophical opposition between order/reason (Apollo) and chaos/intoxication (Dionysos) as drivers of artistic creation.
Ethiopian princess saved by Perseus from a sea monster and who became his wife.

Nom du cours: Aeneas and the founding of Rome (Virgil)
Explication: Fundamental virtue according to Virgil: devotion to the gods, the homeland, and the family. Aeneas is the "pious Aeneas" - he escapes from Troy carrying his old father on his back. This value embodies the Roman ideal in opposition to Greek hybris.

Nom du cours: Aeneas and the founding of Rome (Virgil)
Explication: The Aeneid was written as a commission for Augustus to legitimize the imperial regime by placing Rome within a divine destiny. The lineage of Aeneas, son of Venus, becomes the lineage of Caesar and Augustus himself - a narrative of founding politics as much as literary.

Terme: The cosmology of the Five Suns and the cosmic debt
Explication: The gods had sacrificed their blood to create the fifth sun. Humans were in perpetual debt and had to repay with blood. This logic of cosmic exchange made sacrifices morally necessary in the Aztec vision of the World.
God of the Sun and war, protector of the Mexica. As the sun must "fight" darkness every morning, he needs the blood of captured warriors to complete his daily journey and rise again.

Terme: The Bhagavad Gita as a philosophical text
Explication: The 18 chapters of dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna constitute a major philosophical text, independent of the rest of the epic. Krishna teaches selfless action (karma yoga), devotion (bhakti) and knowledge (jnana) as paths to liberation.

Terme: Orality and the transmission of Indian epics
Explication: Like Homer, The Mahabharata was first an oral epic memorized and recited by griots. Its transcription spanned several centuries. These texts are still recited and sung throughout India, as alive as ever.

Nom du cours: Lancelot, Guinevere and the Round Table
Explication: A social code glorifying the secret and inaccessible love of a knight for a lady (often married). Lancelot and Guinevere are the perfect example of this. This adulterous passion, destructive yet sublime, is at the heart of medieval literature.

Nom du cours: Lancelot, Guinevere and the Round Table
Terme: The Quest for the Grail and medieval Christianity
Explication: The Grail was christianized: the chalice of the Last Supper or the cup that collected the blood of Christ. The quest becomes a spiritual quest for purity. Only Galaad - pure and without sin - can reach it. Lancelot, defiled by his love for Guinevere, fails.

Terme: The figure of the archmage in literature
Explication: Merlin is the prototype of the archmage: Gandalf (Tolkien), Dumbledore (Rowling) are direct descendants. The wise old man with mysterious powers who guides the hero is a near-universal narrative archetype.

The prophecies of Merlin compiled by Geoffrey of Monmouth (1136) became an autonomous literary genre, very popular in the Middle Ages. They were reinterpreted at every major politics Event - like the Apocalypse of John in the Christian World.

Fascination and idealization of the Orient by Europeans, often stereotyped. One Thousand and One Nights, notably in the translation by Antoine Galland (1704), fueled this Orientalism: harems, Caliph, genies became the standard image of the Arab World in Europe.

Narrative Technique: stories are nested within one another. Inherited from the Indian tradition, it was brought to its peak by Scheherazade and would influence Boccaccio, Chaucer, Cervantes, then Borges and postmodern narrative.

From the 7th to the 14th century, Arab merchants dominated maritime trade in the Indian Ocean. The adventures of Sinbad reflect these real networks, exotic goods (spices, silk, porcelain) and the dangers of long-distance navigation.

Terme: Marco Polo as a Western parallel
Explication: Marco Polo (1254-1324) made the inverse journey of Sinbad: from Venice to the China of Kublai Khan. His accounts seemed as fabulous as those of Sinbad. The Book of the Marvels of the World directly influenced Columbus in his plans to travel to Asia.

Nom du cours: The Titans vs the Gods: the complete Titanomachy
Explication: After the Titanomachy, the Olympians had to face the Giants (born from the blood of Uranus), who were nearly invincible. This second war of the gods foreshadows the permanent tensions between Olympian order and the primordial forces of chaos.

Nom du cours: The Titans vs the Gods: the complete Titanomachy
Explication: Prometheus did not participate in the Titanomachy, having foreseen through prophecy that Zeus would win. This neutrality preserved his freedom - which subsequently allowed him to steal fire for humans. His particular position explains his unique role.

Nom du cours: Ra and the creation of the world (Egypt)
Explication: Theological system centered on Heliopolis ("city of the sun"), asserting that Atum/Ra was the primary creator god. It competed with other centers (Memphis: Ptah, Thebes: Amun) whose theologies coexisted and merged.

Nom du cours: Ra and the creation of the world (Egypt)
Explication: Egyptian gods could merge: Ra-Atum, Amun-Ra, Osiris-Ra. This syncretism allowed for the integration of local deities without eliminating them. Egyptian religion was thus inclusive and in perpetual evolution over 3,000 years.

Nom du cours: The birth of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict
Explication: Political Movement founded by Theodor Herzl (The Jewish State, 1896) advocating for the creation of a Jewish national home in response to European antisemitism. He initially proposed Argentina or Uganda before settling on historical Palestine.

Nom du cours: The birth of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict
Explication: Letter from the British minister Balfour promising British support for "the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, while preserving the rights of "non-Jewish communities". This foundational tension has never been resolved.

Starting in 2018, the United States (Trump) imposed massive customs duties on Chinese products, which China responded to in kind. This trade war reflects a technological and geopolitical rivalry deeper than mere trade.

American strategy aiming to separate technological supply chains between the two countries. Sanctions on Huawei and the ban on sales of advanced semiconductors to China reflect the fear of military use of American technologies.

Taiwanese manufacturer producing about 92% of the World's most advanced chips. This global dependence explains why a Chinese invasion would cause a global economic catastrophe - Taiwan's "silicon shield".

American politics which recognizes "one China" without recognizing Beijing's sovereignty over Taiwan, and sells weapons without explicitly promising a military defense. This deliberate ambiguity is supposed to deter invasion while avoiding provoking Beijing.

Krauthammer described (1990) the post-Cold War era as a "unipolar moment" with the United States as the sole superpower. He predicted it would last 30 to 40 years - an accurate prediction, as the "unipolar moment" ended around 2008-2010.

Acronym referring to Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, expanded to several countries since 2024. This grouping embodies multipolarity: powers that reject the Western liberal order without necessarily forming a coherent alternative bloc.

Nom du cours: Oil as a source of conflict
Explication: Economic paradox: countries rich in natural resources (oil, diamonds) often experience lower growth and more frequent conflicts. The oil "rent" creates predatory states and discourages economic diversification.

Nom du cours: Oil as a source of conflict
Explication: Hubbert's theory (1956) predicting that global oil production would reach a summit and then decline. The American shale oil revolution pushed back this limit, but the debate over resource depletion remains central.

Nom du cours: The Suez Canal: why it is strategic
Explication: When Nasser nationalized the canal, France, Great Britain, and Israel invaded Egypt. Under American pressure (Eisenhower threatened to collapse the pound sterling), they had to withdraw - marking the end of Franco-British colonial power.

Nom du cours: The Suez Canal: why it is strategic
Explication: A 400 m container ship that ran aground across the canal for 6 days, blocking 400 ships. It cost the global economy 400 million dollars per hour, perfectly illustrating the strategic importance of the canal in global chains.

Nom du cours: NATO: what is its purpose today?
Terme: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty
Explication: Collective defense clause: an attack against one member is an attack against all. Invoked only once in NATO's history - on September 12, 2001, after 9/11. Its exact scope remains deliberately ambiguous.

Nom du cours: NATO: what is its purpose today?
Explication: Since 1991, NATO has welcomed 14 new members, including former Soviet republics. Russia considers this expansion as an existential threat - an argument used to justify the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Principle adopted by the UN in 2005: the international community can intervene in a sovereign state to protect civilians in danger. Developed in the 1990s after the inaction in Rwanda and Bosnia, its application remains very selective.

The UN includes agencies with specific mandates: WHO (global health), UNICEF (children), FAO (food), UNESCO (culture), UNHCR (refugees). These agencies often achieve concrete results where the Security Council is blocked by a veto.

The Soviet KGB was dissolved in 1991 and replaced by the FSB (domestic) and the SVR (foreign). Putin, a former KGB officer in Dresden, has extensively promoted former KGB members (the “siloviki”) to key positions of power in Russia.

Concept developed by the ideologue Vladislav Surkov: Russia has its own form of democracy adapted to its history, not subject to Western liberal standards. Criticism: this concept actually justifies authoritarianism by rebranding it as “cultural sovereignty”.

Agreement by which Ukraine gave up the 1,900 inherited Soviet nuclear warheads in exchange for security guarantees from Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Russia violated it as early as 2014, which haunts Ukrainian security discussions.

Terme: The Donbas and the separatist republics
Explication: An industrial region in eastern Ukraine where pro-Russian separatists proclaimed “republics” with Russian military support in 2014. This “low-intensity” conflict (14,000 deaths) preceded the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

Contracts by which buyers and sellers commit to a future transaction at a price fixed today. Speculators with no intention of physical delivery represent the vast majority of transactions, amplifying price fluctuations.
Massive boom in American production in the 21st century thanks to hydraulic fracturing, altering the global geopolitical energy balance.

Switzerland maintained absolute banking secrecy for decades, criminally protecting bankers who refused to disclose their clients' identities. This secrecy, eroded since 2010 under international pressure, had made Switzerland the world's leading tax haven.

Tax optimization mechanism: a subsidiary in a normal country "buys" services from a subsidiary in a tax haven at overvalued prices. Profits are thus transferred to the low-tax jurisdiction, reducing the overall tax bill.

Tax structure using Irish and Dutch subsidiaries to transfer intellectual property rights to Bermuda. Apple, Google, and Facebook used it until its phase-out (2020), paying effective rates of less than 2%.

Agreement signed by 136 countries to impose a minimum rate of 15% on the profits of multinationals, regardless of their country of filing. The first major international tax agreement in history, it aims to end the tax "race to the bottom."

Nom du cours: The crisis of the Welfare State
Explication: Document by British economist Beveridge laying the foundations of the Welfare State: universal protection against the "five giants" (poverty, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness). It inspired the creation of the NHS and post-war social systems.

Nom du cours: The crisis of the Welfare State
Explication: By pay-as-you-go: the active workforce finances current retirees. With aging, fewer active workers finance more retirees. By capitalization (funded): individual savings subject to market fluctuations. The debate on the "right" reform is universal in developed countries.

Graph by economist Milanovic: between 1988 and 2008, the Asian middle class and the global ultra-rich progressed the most, while the working class in rich countries stagnated. This curve partly explains the rise of Western populism.

Poor countries export raw materials at low prices and import expensive manufactured goods. This structure inherited from colonialism perpetuates economic dependence: when commodity prices drop, these countries become even poorer.

For Keynes (1936), the State must borrow to spend during recessions. Public debt is an economic management tool, not a moral issue. This Theory justifies stimulus plans like the New Deal or post-COVID stimulus.

An approach stating that a State borrowing in its own currency (United States, Japan) cannot technically go bankrupt - it can always create money. The only risk is inflation. It justifies significant deficits as long as inflation remain under control.

A platform becomes more valuable as the number of users increases. Facebook, Uber, Amazon: the more users there are, the better the service, which attracts even more users - creating almost insurmountable natural monopolies.

An economy of "gig work" where individuals offer their services via platforms without permanent contracts. It weakens traditional social protections (retirement, unemployment) while offering flexibility for workers.

Nom du cours: The role of data (the "oil of the 21st century")
Explication: General Data Protection Regulation - the most ambitious personal data protection Law. It gives European citizens the right to access their data, correct them and delete them. Global companies are subject to its rules.

Nom du cours: The role of data (the "oil of the 21st century")
Explication: Concept by Shoshana Zuboff: GAFAM created a model based on capturing human behaviors to sell them as predictions to advertisers. Humans become the "raw material" of an invisible economic market.

Mobile payment service (2007) allowing money to be sent via SMS without a bank account. Having become the dominant payment system in Kenya and several African countries, it shows that developing countries can "leapfrog" certain technological stages.

A constellation of satellites offering high-speed Internet in areas without terrestrial infrastructure. It can transform Internet access in rural areas of developing countries but remains expensive. Also used by Ukraine in its war against Russia.

Social media algorithms personalize content based on past preferences, creating "bubbles" where each user only sees what confirms their beliefs. This polarizes debates and promotes large-scale disinformation.

A Saint Petersburg troll farm funded by Prigozhin, employing hundreds of people to create fake accounts and manipulate American and European public opinion. Brought to light during the Mueller investigation into the 2016 election.

Nom du cours: The ozone layer hole (and its recovery)
Explication: Synthetic chemical compounds invented in the 1920s, used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants. Chemically stable, they rise into the Stratosphere where they destroy ozone — an effect ignored for decades after their invention.

Nom du cours: The ozone layer hole (and its recovery)
Explication: An international treaty phasing out CFCs, ratified by 197 countries — the only treaty in history ratified by all UN member states. Considered the greatest success of environmental diplomacy.

Benefits that ecosystems provide for free: pollination, water purification, climate regulation, flood prevention. The Dasgupta Review (2021) estimates them at 125 trillion dollars per year — far more than the global GDP.

Thresholds in natural systems beyond which rapid and irreversible changes occur: Arctic ice melt, death of coral reefs, forest dieback. Once these points are passed, returning to the previous state becomes impossible.

Waste management hierarchy in order of priority. First reduce consumption, then reuse existing products, and finally recycle as a last resort. The order is crucial: recycling consumes a lot of energy and does not solve overconsumption.

Industrial strategy consisting of designing products intended to be replaced quickly. Apple, Samsung and many electronic manufacturers are accused of this practice - non-replaceable parts, non-removable batteries, updates forcing the purchase of new devices.

Phenomenon documented since 2006: entire hives disappear without explanation, bees leaving the hive and not returning. The causes are multifactorial: neonicotinoids pesticides, Varroa destructor, loss of habitat, combined pathogens.

Pesticides absorbed by the entire plant, including nectar and pollen, paralyzing the nervous system of insects. Banned for certain crops in Europe since 2018, despite resistance from the agro-industry, they remain authorized in many countries.

Terme: Arctic sea ice and the albedo effect
Explication: Unlike sea ice (the melting of which does not raise water levels), the melting of ice from Greenland and Antarctica makes the oceans rise directly. Furthermore, the dark water replacing the white ice absorbs more heat, accelerating warming.

Storms combined with sea level rise create temporary "storm surges" much higher than the average level. A rise in water levels of 50 cm can multiply the frequency of floods that were described as "100-year floods" by 10 - rare events become common.

English weaving workers who destroyed mechanical weaving machines. Often caricatured as anti-progress, they were actually protesting against the degradation of their working conditions and wages caused by mechanization without social protections.

Regular payment of a fixed sum to all citizens, without conditions. Seen as a response to automation. Experiments in Finland, Kenya and California give encouraging results but their generalization remains highly debated economically.

Nom du cours: Populism: why is it rising everywhere?
Explication: Inglehart and Norris show that populism is as much cultural as economic: the "losers" of globalization and the cultural revolution find themselves in parties that defend their traditional values against a cosmopolitan elite perceived as contemptuous.

Nom du cours: Populism: why is it rising everywhere?
Explication: A concept claimed by Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán (2014): a democratically elected regime that restricts checks and balances (press, justice, NGOs). This model, also practiced by Erdogan and Modi, challenges the notion of liberal democracy.

Nom du cours: Mental health as a societal issue
Explication: A syndrome of chronic exhaustion caused by overwork, recognized by the WHO since 2019 as an occupational phenomenon. It is characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a reduced sense of accomplishment.

Nom du cours: Mental health as a societal issue
Terme: The smartphone and mental health hypothesis (Haidt)
Explication: Psychologist Jonathan Haidt argues that the massive adoption of smartphones by adolescents starting in 2012 is the primary cause of the epidemic of depression and anxiety among young people. The scientific debate remains intense.

Nom du cours: The EU: how does it really work?
Terme: The European Commission and the monopoly of legislative initiative
Explication: Only the Commission (unelected, appointed by governments) can propose European laws. The elected Parliament can amend or reject, but cannot propose legislation itself. This democratic deficit is one of the major structural criticisms of the EU.

Nom du cours: The EU: how does it really work?
Terme: Unanimity in the Council of the EU
Explication: In many areas (taxation, foreign policy), decisions require the unanimity of the 27 Member States. A single state can block – which makes the EU difficult to govern during crises and explains its often-criticized slow decision-making process.
An NGO founded in 1985 that publishes the annual World Press Freedom Index evaluating 180 countries. Its 2024 index places Norway at the top and North Korea and Eritrea at the bottom.

In many democracies, billionaires (Murdoch, Bolloré) have bought up media outlets, raising questions about their independence. In France in 2024, the vast majority of the press is owned by a dozen billionaires.

Terme: The legal vacuum of the "climate refugee"
Explication: The Geneva Convention does not recognize climate displacement as a ground for asylum. People fleeing Sea level rise have no international legal protection - one of the most urgent challenges in current international law.

Terme: The Maldives and nations in danger of extinction
Explication: The Maldive islands, with a maximum altitude of 1.5 m, are threatened with disappearance this century. The Maldivian government has purchased land in Australia as a national relocation plan B - a unique and tragic case in the History of states.

Mechanism by which Bitcoin miners solve complex calculations to validate transactions. This process consumes as much electricity as some countries and is criticized for its colossal environmental footprint.
Pseudonym of the inventor (or group of inventors) of Bitcoin, who published the founding white paper in 2008 and disappeared in 2010. Their identity remains unknown.

Founding treaty of refugee law, signed after the displacements of the Second World War. It defines the refugee and establishes the principle of non-refoulement - the prohibition of expelling someone to a country where their life is threatened.

Cardinal principle of refugee law: no state can return a person to a territory where their life or liberty would be threatened. Recognized as a peremptory norm of international law, it applies even to states that have not ratified the Geneva Convention.

UN agency founded in 1945 whose mandate is to eradicate hunger and ensure Global food security. It collects agricultural statistics, coordinates emergency food aid and promotes sustainable agricultural practices.

Agricultural innovations of the 1960s-70s (new high-yield varieties, chemical fertilizers, irrigation) that multiplied global food production. Norman Borlaug received the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize - The Green Revolution saved hundreds of millions of lives.

Nom du cours: Water: the next source of conflict?
Explication: A situation where water demand exceeds available resources or when water quality limits its use. We speak of severe scarcity below the threshold of 1,000 m³ per inhabitant/year.

Nom du cours: Water: the next source of conflict?
Explication: Dam built by Ethiopia on the Blue Nile since 2011, which will reduce the flow towards Egypt and Sudan. Egypt threatened to go to war if construction continued - an illustration of rising tensions over transboundary water resources.

Concept by theorist Antonio Gramsci: a dominant class maintains its power by making its values accepted as natural and universal. Joseph Nye adapted this idea to international relations with the concept of soft power.

European regulatory standards (GDPR, food standards, environmental standards) are adopted globally by multinationals wishing to access the market of 450 million consumers. The EU thus exercises considerable regulatory soft power.

Digital platforms tend toward natural monopolies: each new user reinforces the value for all others. Competing with Facebook or Amazon becomes almost impossible because their network advantage is insurmountable for a new competitor.

European law aiming to regulate the "gatekeepers" of digital markets. It mandates interoperability and prohibits favoritism of its own services. It is the most ambitious regulation of GAFAM in the world.

Terme: The Paris Agreement (2015) and climate goals
Explication: Treaty signed by 196 countries to limit warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Each country sets its own targets (NDC) - current ambitions lead to approximately 2.5°C of warming according to current projections.

Hydrogen produced by water electrolysis powered by renewable energies. It allows for energy storage and the decarbonization of sectors that are difficult to electrify (steel, cement, aviation). Costly today, it is seen as key for 2050 carbon neutrality.

Each innovation destroys obsolete jobs and creates new ones. History seems to prove Schumpeter right (from the farmer to the driver). The question is whether AI, which also affects skilled jobs, will reproduce this pattern or break it for good.

Reduction of the work week while maintaining salary. Experiments in Iceland, Japan, Spain, and Great Britain show positive results: productivity maintained or improved, increased well-being, reduced absenteeism.

Single party in power since 1949, with 98 million members. It controls the State, the army, the media, and increasingly the economy. The General Secretary (Xi Jinping since 2012) is the true leader of the country.

Unique model: the State directs the market economy via public enterprises, state-owned banks, and five-year plans. Neither pure socialism nor liberal capitalism, it combines market mechanisms with the political control of the Communist Party.
Arab nomads living in the desert, organized into tribes bonded by kinship ties.
Rapid attacks led by tribes against caravans or enemy camps to seize livestock or goods.
Legal status of 'protected' granted to monotheistic non-Muslims living under Islamic authority.
Annual tax paid by non-Muslim populations (subject to the Dhimma) in exchange for the protection of the State.
Edict issued by Muhammad shortly after the Hegira, governing the relations between monotheists (Muslims and Jews) and the clans of the Medina oasis.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Major defeat of the Byzantine Empire against the Seljuk Turks in 1071, causing the loss of Anatolia and the military decline of Byzantium.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Spiritual and social Movement initiated by the Church in the 10th and 11th centuries to limit feudal violence and protect non-combatants.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Ecclesiastical assembly of 1095 during which Urban II launched his call to the crusade.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Popular preacher who led the 'Crusade of the Poor', a disorganized wave preceding that of the barons.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Norman prince from Southern Italy and one of the primary military leaders of the first crusade, founder of the Principality of Antioch.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Title held by Godfrey of Bouillon, who refused the title of King of Jerusalem out of religious humility.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Religious and military order founded in 1119 to protect pilgrims in the Holy Land, becoming a major financial power.

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Sultan of Kurdish origin who unified the Muslim world and retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: A branch of early Christianity, deemed heretical by the Council of Nicaea, which considered that Christ was not equal to God the Father.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Church Father and translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate), witness to the psychological shock caused by the fall of Rome.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Germanic people who seized Roman North Africa and sacked Rome in turn in 455 in a much more devastating manner than Alaric.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Federation of Germanic peoples settled on the lower Rhine, which eventually conquered Gaul under Clovis after the collapse of the Empire.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Germanic people from whom came Odoacer, the military leader who deposed the last Western Emperor.
Germanic people established in Northern Italy from the 6th century onwards, whose kingdom was conquered by Charlemagne in 774.
Nomadic horse-riding people originally from Central Asia, settled in the Danube plain, whose empire was destroyed by Carolingian armies.
Pyrenean pass where the rear-guard of Charlemagne's army was massacred in 778 by the Vascons, an event which inspired the famous 'Song of Roland'.
High local dignitaries appointed by the sovereign to administer a province (the county) in his name, possessing military and judicial powers.
Reference currency imposed by Charlemagne's monetary reform, replacing gold with silver as the basis of the European economic system for several centuries.
King of France (1180-1223) who dismantled the Plantagenet empire by taking Normandy and Maine back from John Lackland.
Decisive battle of 1214 where Philip II Augustus defeated a coalition including England, sealing the fate of John Lackland.
The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution, guaranteeing individual liberties and limiting federal power.
First Lady of the United States and a key figure in the drafting of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
A period of relative economic and politics stability in Eurasia under the Mongol Empire during the 13th and 14th centuries, which unintentionally facilitated the spread of the plague.
A network of trade routes connecting Asia to Europe, the primary vector for the spread of the plague from the East to the Black Sea trading posts.
A Genoese trading post in Crimea (modern-day Feodosia). The siege of the city by the Mongols in 1346 is considered the gateway for the plague into the Mediterranean.
Ancient Greek physician whose theories (notably the theory of humors) dominated medieval medicine, preventing an understanding of the bacterial origin of the plague.
The scientific name for the rat flea, the actual vector of transmission for the Yersinia pestis bacterium from animals to humans.
A fanatical religious movement whose members publicly flogged themselves as a sign of penance to end the epidemic, which was seen as divine punishment.
Pope residing in Avignon during the Black Death. He distinguished himself by protecting Jews from pogroms and by commissioning medical reports on the scourge.
Italian writer who witnessed the plague in Florence. His masterpiece, the Decameron, accurately describes the social and psychological impact of the epidemic on his contemporaries.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: Belief according to which God intervenes directly in human history and politics to fulfill his will.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: Bishop of Beauvais and supporter of the English, he was the architect of the trial sentencing Joan of Arc in Rouen.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: Decisive battle of 1453 which marks the effective end of the Hundred Years' War and the near-total expulsion of the English from the kingdom of France.
Last Byzantine emperor (1449-1453), he died in combat during the final assault on Constantinople.
Elite corps of the Ottoman infantry, originally composed of converted Christian prisoners, renowned for their discipline and loyalty to the Sultan.
Name given to Constantinople after the Ottoman conquest, although the official name did not become Istanbul until the 20th century.
Mythical place of origin of the Aztec peoples, often located in northern present-day Mexico or the southwestern United States.
Fierce enemy people of the Aztecs who became the main military ally of Hernán Cortés during the conquest.
Infectious disease of European origin which was the main agent of mortality during the fall of the Aztec empire.
Language spoken by the Aztecs and still practiced by many communities in Mexico today.
Name given to the Spanish colony established on the ruins of the Aztec empire after 1521.
Greek scholar from the 3rd century BC who was the first to calculate the circumference of the Earth with remarkable precision thanks to the shadow cast by the sun.
Contract signed in April 1492 between Christopher Columbus and the Catholic Monarchs, setting the financial conditions and honorary titles of the navigator in case of success.
A family of wealthy Spanish shipowners, including the brothers Martín Alonso and Vicente Yáñez, who were the true technical and financial supporters of the 1492 expedition.
Indigenous people inhabiting the Greater Antilles at the time of Columbus's arrival; they were the first to suffer the consequences of Spanish colonization.
Powerful merchant tribe that controlled Mecca and the Kaaba at the time of Muhammad.
Successor to Muhammad as head of the Muslim community and the Islamic empire (caliphate).

Nom du cours: Urban II's call and the 1st Crusade (1095)
Explication: Four Christian states (County of Edessa, Principality of Antioch, County of Tripoli, Kingdom of Jerusalem) created by the crusaders in the Near East at the end of the 11th century.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: King of the Visigoths and former officer in the Roman army, he led his people to the capture of Rome in 410 after the failure of negotiations with the Empire.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Western Roman Emperor (395-423) who moved the capital to Ravenna and was unable to prevent the sack of Rome.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Italian city that became the capital of the Western Empire in 402 due to its strategic position protected by marshes.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Theological and philosophical treatise by Saint Augustine written following the sack of Rome to justify Christianity against pagan criticism.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Last Western Roman emperor, deposed at about 15 years of age by the leader Odoacer in 476.

Nom du cours: The Sack of Rome by the Visigoths (410)
Explication: Heruli military leader who overthrew the Western Empire in 476 and established himself as King of Italy under the nominal suzerainty of Constantinople.
Extremely powerful Pope (1198-1216) who excommunicated John Lackland before becoming his ally and annulling the Magna Carta at his request.
Archbishop of Canterbury whose appointment was at the origin of the conflict between John Lackland and the Pope. He played the role of mediator and intellectual architect of the Charter.
17th-century English jurist who reactivated the use of the Magna Carta to oppose the royal absolutism of the Stuarts.
Period of climatic cooling beginning in the 14th century, responsible for poor harvests and famines that weakened the immune resistance of Europeans before the plague.
Mongol empire established on the Russian and Central Asian steppes, whose armies besieged Caffa and introduced the plague to European trading posts.

Nom du cours: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War (1429)
Explication: Faction of the French nobility faithful to the House of Orléans and to the legitimacy of the Valois (Charles VII) during the civil war against the Burgundians.
Estuary flowing into the Bosphorus, forming a protected natural harbor that separated the city of Constantinople from its suburb of Galata.
System of land fortifications of Constantinople erected in the 5th century, famous for its complexity and historical invincibility until 1453.
God of the sun and war among the Aztecs, spiritual guide of the Mexica migration and main beneficiary of human sacrifices.
Last great Aztec ruler reigning during the arrival of Cortés. His hesitant management of the invasion facilitated the capture of Tenochtitlán.
Double pyramid in the center of Tenochtitlán dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc (god of rain), the religious and political heart of the empire.

Conflict (1775-1783) during which France helped the American colonies free themselves from British rule. The financial cost of this support was one of the major causes of the French monarchy's bankruptcy.
A wave of panic and peasant revolt that spread across the French countryside between July and August 1789, leading to the destruction of manorial records.
Mountain range in southwestern Germany from where Mack expected to see Napoleon arrive.
Name given by Napoleon to the French military forces he personally commanded between 1805 and 1814.
Napoleon's tactical maneuver consisting of positioning himself between two enemy armies to face them separately, thus avoiding being overwhelmed by their combined strength.
Massive concentration of cannons advocated by Napoleon to break through enemy lines through intensive bombardment on a specific point.
Post-1815 diplomatic principle aimed at restoring royal dynasties to their thrones at the expense of regimes resulting from the Revolution or the Empire.
Infantry defensive formation composed of several ranks of soldiers forming a rectangle, with bayonnets facing outward to break cavalry charges.
Citizen militia composed mainly of Parisians, with its own weapons and elected leaders. In 1871, it becomes the armed wing of the Commune.
Name given to the supporters of the Paris Commune, as they claimed to belong to a federation of autonomous communes.
Nicknamed the 'Red Virgin', she is one of the major figures of the Commune, an anarchist activist and ambulance driver on the barricades.
Conflict of 1870-1871 which led to the fall of Napoleon III and the unification of Germany, creating lasting French resentment (the loss of Alsace-Lorraine).
Global conflict from 1914 to 1918 that ended European hegemony and radically transformed borders and national societies.
Austrian physician, founder of psychoanalysis. His work 'The Interpretation of Dreams' (1900) marks a major breakthrough in the understanding of the human psyche.
Physical Theory published by Albert Einstein in 1905, overturning the concepts of space and time inherited from classical physics.
Artistic style of the late 19th century characterized by curved lines and patterns inspired by nature, affecting architecture and decoration.
French pictorial movement of the early 20th century favoring bright and arbitrary colors to express emotions rather than reality.
Artistic avant-garde Movement initiated by Picasso and Braque, breaking down objects into simple geometric shapes.
Codename of the German operation on Verdun, meaning "court" or "judgment" in German, illustrating Falkenhayn's will to judge and annihilate the French army.
Town located behind the Verdun front, starting point of the Sacred Way through which supply trucks passed.
System of troop rotation established by Pétain at Verdun, consisting of rotating divisions to the front for a short period to maintain their combat effectiveness.
Territories so devastated by fighting and polluted by unexploded ordnance that the French State prohibited all agricultural activity or Reconstruction there after the war.
Global conflict (1914-1918) that caused the collapse of several empires, including the Russian Empire, which was unable to keep up with the industrial pace of the conflict.
The Russian parliament created after the 1905 revolution. In 1917, it was largely ignored by Tsar Nicholas II.
Calendar used in Russia until 1918, which was 13 days behind the Western Gregorian calendar (hence the discrepancy between February/March and October/November).
Political program presented by Lenin upon his return from exile, advocating for the immediate transition from the bourgeois revolution to the socialist revolution.
Marxist revolutionary and organizer of the Red Army. He was the technical mastermind of the October 1917 insurrection.
Peace treaty signed in March 1918 between Bolshevik Russia and Germany, formalizing the Russian withdrawal from the war at the cost of heavy territorial losses.
A situation where the supply of goods exceeds consumer demand, leading to a drop in prices and an accumulation of useless stock.
Refers to a financial asset (stock or real estate) whose market price is significantly higher than its actual economic value.
A phenomenon where a large number of a bank's customers simultaneously withdraw their deposits for fear of bankruptcy, effectively causing the collapse of the **Institution**.
31st President of the United States (1929-1933), often criticized for his inability to act effectively at the onset of the crisis.
A generalized and lasting fall in prices and wages, which often worsens the crisis by increasing the real burden of debt.
Republican regime in place in Germany between 1919 and 1933, destabilized by economic instability and the rise of extremes.
Liberal economic principle advocating for the absence of state intervention in market mechanisms.
Economic **politics** aimed at stimulating demand and production through increased public spending.
The codename for the **Wehrmacht**'s summer offensive in 1942 targeting the oil fields of the Caucasus.
The German air force, which played a crucial role in the initial bombings of Stalingrad.
Head of the Luftwaffe, he wrongly promised Hitler that his aircraft could resupply the encircled 6th Army by air.
Hungarian-born physicist who conceived the idea of a nuclear chain reaction and convinced Einstein to write to Roosevelt to launch the American atomic program.
New Mexico desert where the Trinity test was conducted, chosen for its geographical isolation.
Suicide attack units of the Imperial Japanese Army that crashed their planes into Allied ships to cause as much damage as possible.
Conference held in July 1945 where the Allies (Truman, Stalin, Churchill/Attlee) discussed the fate of Japan and postwar Europe.
Name of the B-29 bomber that dropped the 'Fat Man' atomic bomb on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945.
Primary target designated for the second atomic bombing, saved by weather conditions that forced the pilot to head towards Nagasaki.
Radio address recorded by Emperor Hirohito and broadcast on August 15, 1945, announcing the unconditional surrender of Japan.
Japanese term referring to the survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, victims of physical after-effects and discrimination.
Strategic doctrine based on the threat of using nuclear weapons to prevent an adversary from launching an attack.
1896 Supreme Court ruling that validated segregationist laws under the 'separate but equal' principle.
Socialist training and civil rights education center in Tennessee where Rosa Parks learned methods of non-violent resistance.
Historic federal law that ended all forms of racial segregation in public places and banned employment discrimination.
Codename for the secret Soviet operation to deploy troops, aircraft, and nuclear missiles to Cuba in 1962.
Period of the Cold War (1962-1979) characterized by a desire for dialogue, peaceful coexistence and nuclear arms limitation treaties.
NATO member country where the United States had installed Jupiter missiles, constituting one of the reasons for the Soviet response in Cuba.
Soviet intermediate-range ballistic missiles deployed in Cuba, capable of reaching most of the American territory.

Unlike the protectorates (Morocco, Tunisia), Algeria had been divided since 1848 into three French departments attached to the Ministry of the Interior. Any independence was therefore legally considered a secession from the national territory.
Law passed in 1956 by the French Parliament entrusting the army with full police powers in Algeria to fight against the nationalist insurrection.
Asymmetric combat Technique practiced by the FLN, based on ambushes, attacks and the use of the population as a refuge, faced with a more powerful conventional army.
Failed coup attempt in Algiers in April 1961 by four generals (Challe, Jouhaud, Zeller, Salan) opposed to Charles de Gaulle's politics of self-determination.
Organisation de l'Armée Secrète. Clandestine terrorist organization supporting French Algeria which increased the number of attacks to prevent independence between 1961 and 1962.
Official end of military hostilities between two warring forces.
Muslim fighters recruited as auxiliaries in the French army. Abandoned by France in 1962, thousands were massacred in Algeria or confined to camps in mainland France.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: Founder of the Vietnamese Communist Party and the Viet Minh league. A leading figure in Vietnam's independence, he became the president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: Northern part of present-day Vietnam, centered around Hanoi. It was the historical heart of the Viet Minh resistance during the Indochina War.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: System of seasonal winds in Southeast Asia causing torrential rainfall from May to October, turning the Dien Bien Phu terrain into an impassable swamp.

Nom du cours: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu (1954)
Explication: Conflict (1955-1975) pitting North Vietnam (communist) against South Vietnam (supported by the United States), prolonging the tensions born from the 1954 division.
Ottoman administrative system organizing populations by religious denominations, offering a certain autonomy to minorities protected by the sultan.
Nationalist political party (Committee of Union and Progress) that took power in 1908 and radicalized its politics towards a Pan-Turkism excluding Christian minorities.
Dispersion of a people across the World after exile from their homeland. The Armenian diaspora was born from the flight of genocide survivors.
Physical, intentional, systematic, and programmed extermination of a human group because of its ethnic, religious, or social origins.
Attempt to regulate international relations through common rules and shared institutions to solve problems that cross the borders of a single State.
Military personnel made available to the UN by member States to conduct peacekeeping operations in conflict zones.
Foreign politics doctrine consisting of a State not intervening in the affairs of the World in order to preserve its independence and its immediate interests.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Explication: Speech delivered on May 9, 1950, by Robert Schuman, considered the birth certificate of European construction.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Explication: Common Agricultural Policy, set up in 1962 to ensure Europe's food self-sufficiency and modernize its agriculture.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Explication: Supranational executive body of the ECSC, ancestor of the current European Commission, independent of national governments.

Nom du cours: The birth of the EU: from the ECSC to Maastricht
Explication: Economic area without customs borders where the four freedoms of movement (goods, people, services, capital) apply.
Political and military movement formed by Tutsi exiles in Uganda. Led by Paul Kagame, it launched the offensive that ended the genocide in July 1994.
Extremist ideology advocating Hutu supremacy and the physical elimination of Tutsis, considered foreign invaders.
Reference to the Battle of Mogadishu (1993) where American soldiers were killed, which cooled any willingness for American military intervention in Africa.
French military operation launched in June 1994 under a UN mandate, officially humanitarian, but whose role regarding fleeing perpetrators of the genocide remains controversial.
Former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where millions of Hutus (refugees and perpetrators of the genocide) fled after the victory of the RPF.
Rwandan community courts established to judge the perpetrators of the genocide and promote national reconciliation.
Jurisdiction established by the UN based in Arusha (Tanzania) to try the high-ranking officials responsible for the genocide.

Nom du cours: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
Explication: German Democratic Republic, a socialist state created in 1949 in the Soviet occupation zone, with East Berlin as its capital.

Nom du cours: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
Explication: Expression popularized by Winston Churchill referring to the physical and ideological border separating Europe under Soviet influence from Western Europe.

Nom du cours: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
Explication: Peaceful protest Movement in Czechoslovakia (November-December 1989) which led to the end of the communist regime without major violence.
Name of the German army between 1935 and 1945, including the land army, the navy, and the air force.
Main application point of military effort during an offensive, aiming to concentrate force on a narrow area to break the front.
European Recovery Program, official name of the reconstruction program better known as the Marshall Plan.
Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, created in 1948 to coordinate the distribution of Marshall Plan aid among recipient countries.
European Economic Community, the predecessor of the European Union, whose beginnings of economic cooperation date back to the collective management of the Marshall Plan.
Conflict (1946-1954) pitting France against the communist Viet Minh, resulting in French defeat and the independence of its former colonies.
Massive aerial bombardment campaign conducted by the US Air Force against North Vietnam between 1965 and 1968.
Military strategy aiming to flush out insurgents in the jungle to eliminate them through firepower rather than holding territorial positions.
Headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, by extension the American military command.
Massacre of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians by American soldiers in 1968, the revelation of which shocked world opinion.
